Actions on Objectives
Detected
Reconnaissance. Attacker researches the target — OSINT, scanning, enumeration. → [LLM] Internet-exposed IPMI/BMC management plane on UDP 623 (CVE-2013-4786 exposure) · Asset exposure — vulnerability matches article CVE(s)
Weaponization. Coupling exploit code with deliverable payload (e.g. weaponized PDF/Office doc, trojanized installer).
Delivery. Transmitting the weapon (phishing email, USB, watering hole, drive-by, malicious ad).
Exploitation. Triggering the exploit — vulnerability/macro/trust abuse to execute code. → [LLM] External IPMI RAKP hash-harvest sweep across many BMCs (UDP 623 fan-out)
Installation. Establishing persistence on the host — backdoor, service, scheduled task, registry key.
Command & Control. Beacon to attacker infrastructure for control and tasking.
Actions on Objectives. Lateral movement, credential dumping, data theft, ransomware, sabotage. → [LLM] Internal host sweeping management plane on UDP 623 (compromised BMC pivot) · Ransomware-style mass file rename / extension change · LSASS process access / dump (credential theft) · Remote service execution — PsExec / SMB lateral movement
Internet-exposed IPMI/BMC management plane on UDP 623 (CVE-2013-4786 exposure) AIReconnaissance Medium
Hunts inbound UDP/623 (IPMI RMCP) reaching internal server BMC listeners from public source IPs, the exposure precondition for CVE-2013-4786 RAKP hash disclosure. Surfaces every internet-reachable BMC/iLO/IPMI interface so the SOC can inventory and isolate them before an attacker harvests a hash. Rationale: Anchors on IPMI's fixed UDP/623 RMCP port reaching internal BMC listeners (LocalPort==623) from public IPs — the exact exposure the article measured (36,872 hosts on UDP 623). Defender only sees this on Supermicro-style shared-LAN BMCs sharing the host NIC; perimeter firewall (Sentinel/Splunk) is the authoritative source, hence the pairing. Cross-checked against: • https://nvd.nist.gov/vuln/detail/cve-2013-4786 • https://www.tenable.com/plugins/nessus/80101 • https://www.rapid7.com/blog/post/2013/07/02/a-penetration-testers-guide-to-ipmi/
ATT&CKT1046 T1595.001
Data sourcesNetwork_Traffic.All_Traffic
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Authorized vulnerability scanners (Nessus/Qualys/Rapid7) probing UDP 623 from a scanning appliance
  • Managed-service-provider remote BMC management from a known external NOC range
  • Datacenter DCIM/monitoring platform polling BMCs across a site-to-site link that egresses to a public IP
  • Internet-based backup/OOB console vendor legitimately reaching iLO/IPMI
Suppression filter
| where SourceIP !in ("<sanctioned_scanner_ip>")  // replace with your scanner appliance list; keep query runnable without it by leaving the in() populated at deploy
Response runbook
1) TRIAGE: Identify the internal DestinationIP as a BMC (Supermicro/iLO/IPMI). Confirm whether the SourceIP is a sanctioned scanner or MSP range; if unknown/foreign, treat as hostile reconnaissance. 2) CONTAIN: Block UDP/623 inbound at the perimeter for that BMC and move the management interface onto an isolated VLAN; rotate the factory BMC password immediately (ADMIN + 10-char sticker default). 3) HUNT: Pivot to UC2 to check whether the same SourceIP swept multiple BMCs, and to the BMC's own auth logs for successful 'ADMIN'/empty-username logins indicating the hash was already cracked.
DeviceNetworkEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(24h)
| where LocalPort == 623
| where RemoteIPType == "Public"
| summarize FirstSeen=min(Timestamp), LastSeen=max(Timestamp), Attempts=count(), Sources=dcount(RemoteIP), SampleSources=make_set(RemoteIP, 25) by DeviceName, LocalIP, LocalPort
| order by Attempts desc
CommonSecurityLog
| where TimeGenerated > ago(24h)
| where DestinationPort == 623
| where ipv4_is_private(DestinationIP) and not(ipv4_is_private(SourceIP))
| summarize FirstSeen=min(TimeGenerated), LastSeen=max(TimeGenerated), Hits=count() by SourceIP, DestinationIP, DeviceProduct, DeviceAction
| order by Hits desc
title: Internet-Sourced IPMI RMCP Traffic to Internal BMC (UDP 623)
id: 8b1e4c2a-3d5f-4a91-9b2c-7e6f0a1d2c34
description: Detects inbound UDP/623 IPMI RMCP connections to internal management controllers from external sources, exposure vector for CVE-2013-4786 RAKP hash disclosure.
references:

level: medium

External IPMI RAKP hash-harvest sweep across many BMCs (UDP 623 fan-out) AIExploitation High
Detects a single external source touching many distinct internal BMCs on UDP/623 in a short window — the RAKP message-1/message-2 hash-harvesting sweep behind CVE-2013-4786. Fan-out across dozens of management controllers distinguishes mass hash-collection from a single admin session. Rationale: The article's core behaviour is offline hash harvesting at scale (24,650 of 36,872 hosts leaked material); the detectable network signature is one source fanning out to many UDP/623 BMCs. The dcount(dest) threshold isolates the sweep from a legitimate single-BMC admin session and is high-fidelity because no benign workflow touches 20+ distinct BMCs from one external IP. Cross-checked against: • https://nvd.nist.gov/vuln/detail/cve-2013-4786 • https://security.netapp.com/advisory/ntap-20190919-0005/ • https://www.rapid7.com/blog/post/2013/07/02/a-penetration-testers-guide-to-ipmi/
ATT&CKT1212 T1110.002
Data sourcesNetwork_Traffic.All_Traffic
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • A centralized monitoring/DCIM server (Zabbix, Redfish poller, ipmitool cron) whose traffic egresses via NAT to a public IP and legitimately polls every BMC
  • Authorized external pentest or scheduled ASM (attack-surface-management) scan of the datacenter
  • MSP fleet-management platform performing bulk firmware/health checks across all controllers
  • Cloud provider BMC orchestration reaching many tenant management controllers
Suppression filter
| where SourceIP !in ("<monitoring_nat_egress_ip>", "<asm_scanner_ip>")  // populate with sanctioned monitoring/ASM egress IPs at deploy
Response runbook
1) TRIAGE: Confirm the SourceIP is external and not a NAT'd internal monitoring server; check geolocation/ASN and whether the fan-out count spikes vs the 30-day baseline. 2) CONTAIN: Null-route/deny the SourceIP at the perimeter, block UDP/623 inbound org-wide, and force a factory-BMC-password rotation across every swept controller (assume hashes captured). 3) HUNT: Correlate follow-on successful BMC logins with 'ADMIN' or empty usernames, review iLO/IPMI for unexpected firmware-update or virtual-media mount events, and check for lateral reuse of the same credential across other management interfaces.
DeviceNetworkEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(24h)
| where LocalPort == 623
| where RemoteIPType == "Public"
| summarize BMCsHit=dcount(DeviceName), Attempts=count(), FirstSeen=min(Timestamp), LastSeen=max(Timestamp), Targets=make_set(DeviceName, 50) by RemoteIP
| where BMCsHit >= 5   // 5 monitored shared-LAN BMCs from one external IP = sweep, not a single admin
| order by BMCsHit desc
CommonSecurityLog
| where TimeGenerated > ago(24h)
| where DestinationPort == 623
| where not(ipv4_is_private(SourceIP))
| summarize BMCsHit=dcount(DestinationIP), Attempts=count(), FirstSeen=min(TimeGenerated), LastSeen=max(TimeGenerated), Targets=make_set(DestinationIP, 50) by SourceIP
| where BMCsHit >= 20   // one external IP hitting 20+ distinct BMCs on UDP 623 = mass RAKP harvest
| order by BMCsHit desc
NETWORK
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
| tstats `summariesonly` count dc(All_Traffic.dest_ip) as bmc_count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime from datamodel=Network_Traffic.All_Traffic where All_Traffic.dest_port=623 All_Traffic.transport=udp by All_Traffic.src_ip _time span=1h
| `drop_dm_object_name(All_Traffic)`
| where bmc_count >= 20
| `security_content_ctime(firstTime)` | `security_content_ctime(lastTime)`
| sort - bmc_count
| tstats summariesonly=false count dc(All_Traffic.dest_ip) as bmc_count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime from datamodel=Network_Traffic.All_Traffic where All_Traffic.dest_port=623 All_Traffic.transport=udp by All_Traffic.src_ip _time span=1h
| `drop_dm_object_name(All_Traffic)`
| where bmc_count >= 20
| `security_content_ctime(firstTime)` | `security_content_ctime(lastTime)`
| sort - bmc_count
Internal host sweeping management plane on UDP 623 (compromised BMC pivot) AIActions on Objectives Medium
Detects a monitored internal host initiating UDP/623 IPMI connections to many distinct internal management controllers — the pivot the article describes when one cracked BMC credential is reused across the broader management plane. Flags ipmitool-style sweeps from workstations/servers that have no business enumerating BMCs. Rationale: Article states 'a single compromised BMC could serve as a pivot point to the broader management plane' with credential reuse across interfaces. The detectable pivot is an internal, non-machine-account host emitting UDP/623 to 10+ internal BMCs — normal admins touch one or a handful, so the fan-out plus surfacing InitiatingProcessFileName (catches ipmitool.exe/rakp harvesters) is the high-fidelity signal. Cross-checked against: • https://www.rapid7.com/blog/post/2013/07/02/a-penetration-testers-guide-to-ipmi/ • https://nvd.nist.gov/vuln/detail/cve-2013-4786
ATT&CKT1210 T1046
Data sourcesNetwork_Traffic.All_Traffic
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Sanctioned monitoring server or DCIM node (Zabbix/Nagios/Redfish poller) running ipmitool sweeps on a schedule
  • Firmware-management automation (e.g. Supermicro SUM, HPE iLO Amplifier) enumerating controllers for a maintenance window
  • A jump/bastion host in the management VLAN legitimately reaching many BMCs
  • Infrastructure-as-code health checks (Ansible ipmi modules) during a deploy
Suppression filter
| where DeviceName !in~ ("MON-IPMI-01", "DCIM-POLLER-01") and InitiatingProcessFileName !in~ ("zabbix_agentd.exe", "sum.exe")  // replace with your sanctioned monitoring hosts/tools at deploy
Response runbook
1) TRIAGE: Identify the initiating host and InitiatingProcessFileName — is it a known monitoring node or an unexpected workstation/server? Confirm the account is human and not a sanctioned service account. 2) CONTAIN: Isolate the host if it is not an authorized management node, kill the ipmitool/enumeration process, and disable the account's access to the management VLAN; assume any BMC creds it used are compromised and rotate them. 3) HUNT: Trace which BMCs answered, check those controllers for new logins, firmware-update or virtual-media events, and look for the same host performing UDP/623 to additional segments or reusing recovered credentials against other management interfaces.
DeviceNetworkEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(24h)
| where RemotePort == 623
| where RemoteIPType == "Private"
| where InitiatingProcessAccountName !endswith "$"
| summarize BMCsTargeted=dcount(RemoteIP), Attempts=count(), Targets=make_set(RemoteIP, 50), FirstSeen=min(Timestamp), LastSeen=max(Timestamp) by DeviceName, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessAccountName
| where BMCsTargeted >= 10   // one host hitting 10+ internal BMCs on IPMI = management-plane sweep
| order by BMCsTargeted desc
ImNetworkSession
| where TimeGenerated > ago(24h)
| where DstPortNumber == 623
| where NetworkProtocol =~ "UDP"
| where ipv4_is_private(DstIpAddr)
| summarize BMCsTargeted=dcount(DstIpAddr), Attempts=count(), Targets=make_set(DstIpAddr, 50), FirstSeen=min(TimeGenerated), LastSeen=max(TimeGenerated) by SrcIpAddr, SrcHostname
| where BMCsTargeted >= 10
| order by BMCsTargeted desc

Asset exposure — vulnerability matches article CVE(s) Reconnaissance High
Match vulnerability scanner output to the CVE(s) named in the article.
ATT&CKT1190
Data sourcesVulnerabilities DeviceInfo DeviceTvmSoftwareVulnerabilities
// TVM tables are daily snapshots — pin a 1-day window so the engine
// partitions on Timestamp instead of scanning the full retention.
DeviceTvmSoftwareVulnerabilities
| where Timestamp > ago(1d)
| where CveId in~ ("CVE-2013-4786")
| join kind=inner (DeviceInfo | where Timestamp > ago(1d)) on DeviceId
| project DeviceName, OSPlatform, CveId, VulnerabilitySeverityLevel, RecommendedSecurityUpdate
| order by VulnerabilitySeverityLevel asc, DeviceName asc

// Sentinel has no native TVM table. If MDE→Sentinel streaming is enabled,
// `DeviceTvmSoftwareVulnerabilities` is available. Otherwise this UC has
// no Sentinel translation — track via Update / Heartbeat OS-version
// gaps as a coarse approximation.
DeviceTvmSoftwareVulnerabilities
| where TimeGenerated > ago(1d)
| where CveId in~ ("CVE-2013-4786")
| join kind=inner (DeviceInfo | where TimeGenerated > ago(1d)) on DeviceId
| project DeviceName, OSPlatform, CveId,
          VulnerabilitySeverityLevel, RecommendedSecurityUpdate
| order by VulnerabilitySeverityLevel asc, DeviceName asc
APPLICATION
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
| tstats `summariesonly` count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime
    from datamodel=Vulnerabilities
    where Vulnerabilities.signature IN ("CVE-2013-4786")
    by Vulnerabilities.dest, Vulnerabilities.signature, Vulnerabilities.severity, Vulnerabilities.cve
| `drop_dm_object_name(Vulnerabilities)`
| sort - severity
| tstats summariesonly=false count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime
    from datamodel=Vulnerabilities
    where Vulnerabilities.signature IN ("CVE-2013-4786")
    by Vulnerabilities.dest, Vulnerabilities.signature, Vulnerabilities.severity, Vulnerabilities.cve
| `drop_dm_object_name(Vulnerabilities)`
| sort - severity
Ransomware-style mass file rename / extension change Actions on Objectives Medium
Threshold detection: many files renamed in short window, often with new extension.
ATT&CKT1486
Data sourcesEndpoint.Filesystem DeviceFileEvents
DeviceFileEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(1d)
| where InitiatingProcessAccountName !endswith "$"
| where ActionType in ("FileRenamed","FileModified")
| summarize files = dcount(FileName) by DeviceName, InitiatingProcessAccountName, bin(Timestamp, 1m)
| where files > 200    // empirical: > 200 unique-file renames in 1m by one account on one host
                       //            is well above the P99 of legitimate bulk-tooling
| order by files desc

ImFileEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(1d)
| where ActorUsername !endswith "$"
| where EventType in ("FileRenamed","FileModified")
| summarize files = dcount(TargetFileName)
            by DvcHostname, ActorUsername, ActingProcessName, bin(TimeGenerated, 1m)
| where files > 200    // P99 of legit bulk-tooling per-minute rename volume
| order by files desc
ENDPOINT
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
| tstats `summariesonly` count, dc(Filesystem.file_name) AS files
    from datamodel=Endpoint.Filesystem
    where Filesystem.action IN ("modified","renamed")
    by Filesystem.dest, Filesystem.user, _time span=1m
| `drop_dm_object_name(Filesystem)`
| where files > 200
| sort - files
| tstats summariesonly=false count, dc(Filesystem.file_name) AS files
    from datamodel=Endpoint.Filesystem
    where Filesystem.action IN ("modified","renamed")
    by Filesystem.dest, Filesystem.user, _time span=1m
| `drop_dm_object_name(Filesystem)`
| where files > 200
| sort - files
LSASS process access / dump (credential theft) Actions on Objectives High
Mimikatz, comsvcs.dll MiniDump, or any non-Windows process opening LSASS.
ATT&CKT1003.001 T1003
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes DeviceEvents
DeviceEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where AccountName !endswith "$"
| where ActionType == "OpenProcessApiCall"
| where FileName =~ "lsass.exe"
| where InitiatingProcessFileName !in~ ("MsSense.exe","MsMpEng.exe","csrss.exe",
                                          "svchost.exe","wininit.exe","services.exe",
                                          "lsm.exe","SearchProtocolHost.exe")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, ActionType, FileName,
          InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine,
          InitiatingProcessFolderPath, AccountName
| order by Timestamp desc
// SecurityEvent EventID 4663 = object access. AccessMask 0x10 / 0x40 / 0x1010
// indicate read access to lsass.exe — credential-dump signature. Audit
// Object Access > Audit File System policy required.
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where EventID == 4663
| where ObjectName endswith "\lsass.exe"
| where Account !endswith "$"
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, Account, ObjectName, ProcessName,
          AccessMask, AccessReason
| order by TimeGenerated desc

title: LSASS Process Access Outside Microsoft-Signed Tooling
id: 7c8b2e10-4d4f-4a8c-9c1f-bf6e2c4a8d04
status: experimental
description: |
    Anything opening lsass.exe with read-memory access that isn't a
    Microsoft signed component (Defender, csrss, etc.) is suspect.
    Mimikatz / Pypykatz / nanodump signature.
references:
    - https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1003/001/
author: Clankerusecase
date: 2026/05/02
tags:
    - attack.t1003.001
    - attack.credential-access
logsource:
    category: process_access
    product: windows
detection:
    selection:
        TargetImage|endswith: '\lsass.exe'
    filter_known_good:
        SourceImage|endswith:
            - '\MsSense.exe'
            - '\MsMpEng.exe'
            - '\csrss.exe'
            - '\svchost.exe'
            - '\wininit.exe'
            - '\services.exe'
            - '\lsm.exe'
            - '\SearchProtocolHost.exe'
    condition: selection and not filter_known_good
falsepositives:
    - Third-party EDR / forensic tools — extend the filter list
level: high
ENDPOINT
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
| tstats `summariesonly` count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime
    from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
    where (Processes.process="*lsass*" OR Processes.process="*sekurlsa*"
        OR Processes.process="*MiniDump*" OR Processes.process="*comsvcs.dll*MiniDump*"
        OR Processes.process="*procdump*lsass*")
       OR (Processes.process_name="rundll32.exe" AND Processes.process="*comsvcs*MiniDump*")
    by Processes.dest, Processes.user, Processes.process_name, Processes.process, Processes.parent_process_name
| `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)`
| tstats summariesonly=false count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime
    from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
    where (Processes.process="*lsass*" OR Processes.process="*sekurlsa*"
        OR Processes.process="*MiniDump*" OR Processes.process="*comsvcs.dll*MiniDump*"
        OR Processes.process="*procdump*lsass*")
       OR (Processes.process_name="rundll32.exe" AND Processes.process="*comsvcs*MiniDump*")
    by Processes.dest, Processes.user, Processes.process_name, Processes.process, Processes.parent_process_name
| `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)`
Remote service execution — PsExec / SMB lateral movement Actions on Objectives High
psexec / paexec / smbexec / wmic /node — service install over SMB from remote host.
ATT&CKT1021.002 T1569.002
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes DeviceProcessEvents
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where AccountName !endswith "$"
| where FileName in~ ("psexec.exe","psexesvc.exe","paexec.exe","smbexec.py")
   or (FileName =~ "wmic.exe" and ProcessCommandLine has "/node:")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, FileName, ProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessFileName
| order by Timestamp desc

SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where EventID == 4688            // process-create (audit-policy required)
| where Account !endswith "$"
| where NewProcessName endswith "\psexec.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\psexesvc.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\paexec.exe"
   or (NewProcessName endswith "\wmic.exe" and CommandLine has "/node:")
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, Account, NewProcessName, CommandLine,
          ParentProcessName
| order by TimeGenerated desc

title: PsExec / SMB Lateral Movement Tooling Execution
id: 7c8b2e10-4d4f-4a8c-9c1f-bf6e2c4a8d03
status: experimental
description: |
    PsExec, paexec, smbexec, csexec, remcom — admin-grade tooling that
    pivots over SMB. Pair with `wmic /node:` for the full cluster.
references:
    - https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1021/002/
    - https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1569/002/
author: Clankerusecase
date: 2026/05/02
tags:

    - attack.t1569.002
    - attack.lateral-movement
    - attack.execution
logsource:
    category: process_creation
    product: windows
detection:
    selection_psexec:
        Image|endswith:
            - '\psexec.exe'
            - '\psexec64.exe'
            - '\psexesvc.exe'
            - '\paexec.exe'
            - '\csexec.exe'
            - '\remcom.exe'
            - '\smbexec.py'
    selection_wmic_remote:
        Image|endswith:
            - '\wmic.exe'
        CommandLine|contains:
            - '/node:'
    condition: selection_psexec or selection_wmic_remote
falsepositives:
    - Sysadmins running approved remote-management tooling — wrap with
      a known-admin-host watchlist
level: high
ENDPOINT
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
| tstats `summariesonly` count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime
    from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
    where Processes.process_name IN ("psexec.exe","psexesvc.exe","paexec.exe","smbexec.py")
       OR (Processes.process_name="wmic.exe" AND Processes.process="*/node:*")
    by Processes.dest, Processes.user, Processes.process_name, Processes.process, Processes.parent_process_name
| `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)`
| tstats summariesonly=false count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime
    from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
    where Processes.process_name IN ("psexec.exe","psexesvc.exe","paexec.exe","smbexec.py")
       OR (Processes.process_name="wmic.exe" AND Processes.process="*/node:*")
    by Processes.dest, Processes.user, Processes.process_name, Processes.process, Processes.parent_process_name
| `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)`
Critical

Nimbus Manticore Deploys NightLedger and Turns Victim Systems Into Covert Relays

The Hacker News
2026-07-28 8 use cases 4 techniques 6 kill-chain phases detected

The Iranian state-backed hacking group tracked as Nimbus Manticore (aka GalaxyGato, Mirage Kitten, Smoke Sandstorm, Subtle Snail, and UNC1549) has been attributed to a fresh set of attacks targeting entities across the Middle East, Africa, and South Asia. The intrusions involve the use of a previously undocumented Windows backdoor called NightLedger and two custom WebSocket tunnelers,

Actions on Objectives

Reconnaissance. Attacker researches the target — OSINT, scanning, enumeration.
Weaponization. Coupling exploit code with deliverable payload (e.g. weaponized PDF/Office doc, trojanized installer).
Delivery. Transmitting the weapon (phishing email, USB, watering hole, drive-by, malicious ad). → Phishing-link click correlated to endpoint execution · Email attachment opened from external sender
Exploitation. Triggering the exploit — vulnerability/macro/trust abuse to execute code. → Office app spawning script/LOLBin child process · Fake CAPTCHA / clipboard-injected PowerShell (ClickFix / FakeCaptcha) · Article-specific behavioural hunt — Nimbus Manticore Deploys NightLedger and Turns Victim Systems Into Covert Relays
Installation. Establishing persistence on the host — backdoor, service, scheduled task, registry key. → [LLM] Nimbus Manticore BridgeHead/NightLedger side-load: unbcl.dll loaded outside System32
Command & Control. Beacon to attacker infrastructure for control and tasking. → Beaconing — periodic outbound to small set of destinations
Actions on Objectives. Lateral movement, credential dumping, data theft, ransomware, sabotage. → [LLM] NightLedger collection of domain-join diagnostics (C:\Windows\debug\NetSetup.log)
Nimbus Manticore BridgeHead/NightLedger side-load: unbcl.dll loaded outside System32 AIInstallation High
Hunts the malicious 'unbcl.dll' (BridgeHead SOCKS5 tunneler / NightLedger loader, variants like unbcl-new6.dll) side-loaded by a host binary from a writable directory. The legitimate Windows unbcl.dll only lives under System32/SysWOW64/WinSxS, so any load from elsewhere is anomalous and article-specific to UNC1549's side-loading chain. Rationale: unbcl.dll is a genuine Windows System32 DLL; Kaspersky/Securelist confirm BridgeHead is delivered as 'unbcl.dll' (variant 'unbcl-new6.dll'). Anchoring on the file name + a non-System32 load path yields a high-fidelity side-load signal without needing hashes. Cross-checked against: • https://securelist.com/the-gentlemen-raas/120447/ • https://www.nextron-systems.com/2026/06/01/detecting-nimbus-manticore-and-their-sideloading-infection-chains/ • https://research.checkpoint.com/2026/fast-and-furious-nimbus-manticore-operations-during-the-iranian-conflict/
ATT&CKT1574.002
Data sourcesEndpoint.Filesystem
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Windows servicing/WinSxS component staging that copies unbcl.dll during a feature update
  • Third-party backup software bundling a private copy of a similarly named DLL
  • Security-tool sandbox or forensic imaging that reconstructs System DLLs in a scratch directory
  • Developer/build machines with a checked-out Windows SDK sample referencing unbcl
  • Application virtualization (App-V/MSIX) mounting system DLLs under a package root
Suppression filter
| where InitiatingProcessFileName !in~ ("TiWorker.exe","TrustedInstaller.exe","msiexec.exe") and InitiatingProcessFolderPath !has @"\WinSxS\"
Response runbook
Step 1 (triage): Pull the SHA256 of the loaded unbcl.dll and the host process (InitiatingProcessFileName/FolderPath); confirm the host is a legitimately-signed EXE running from a writable/non-standard folder and that the DLL is unsigned or signed by an unexpected CA. Step 2 (contain): Isolate the host, kill the side-load host process, and quarantine both the host EXE and unbcl.dll; block the C2 once identified. Step 3 (hunt): Sweep the fleet for the same DLL name/hash, look for the sibling NetSetup.log collection behavior, and check for outbound WebSocket/HTTPS relay traffic (BridgeHead/ArcBridge) from the same process.
DeviceImageLoadEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where FileName startswith "unbcl" and FileName endswith ".dll"
| where not (FolderPath startswith @"C:\Windows\System32" or FolderPath startswith @"C:\Windows\SysWOW64" or FolderPath has @"\WinSxS\")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, InitiatingProcessAccountName,
          LoadedDll = FileName, LoadedFrom = FolderPath, SHA256,
          HostProcess = InitiatingProcessFileName, HostPath = InitiatingProcessFolderPath,
          InitiatingProcessCommandLine
| order by Timestamp desc
ImFileEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where EventType == "FileCreated"
| where TargetFileName startswith "unbcl" and TargetFileName endswith ".dll"
| where not (TargetFilePath startswith @"C:\Windows\System32" or TargetFilePath startswith @"C:\Windows\SysWOW64" or TargetFilePath has @"\WinSxS\")
| project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, ActorUsername, DroppedBy = ActingProcessName,
          ActingProcessCommandLine, TargetFilePath, TargetFileSHA256
| order by TimeGenerated desc

description: Detects the Windows unbcl.dll (or variant such as unbcl-new6.dll) being loaded from a path other than System32/SysWOW64/WinSxS, indicative of UNC1549 BridgeHead/NightLedger DLL side-loading.

#event_simpleName=FileWritten TargetFileName=/\\unbcl[^\\]*\.dll$/i
| NOT TargetFileName=/\\(System32|SysWOW64|WinSxS)\\/i

NightLedger collection of domain-join diagnostics (C:\Windows\debug\NetSetup.log) AIActions on Objectives Medium
Hunts access to C:\Windows\debug\NetSetup.log, a domain-join troubleshooting log NightLedger specifically harvests alongside a process listing for reconnaissance. This file is almost never read outside of a domain-join operation, making any harvest of it a strong, campaign-specific signal. Rationale: C:\Windows\debug\NetSetup.log is an explicit, article-named collection target of NightLedger. It is written only during domain-join operations and virtually never read afterward, so a process reading/referencing it is a high-signal recon indicator; the Falcon FileOpenInfo path catches the in-DLL read, other platforms catch operator/LOLBin references. Cross-checked against: • https://securelist.com/the-gentlemen-raas/120447/ • https://industrialcyber.co/ransomware/irgc-linked-nimbus-manticore-group-attacks-defense-aerospace-telecom-sectors-using-minifast-malware-toolkit/
ATT&CKT1005 T1016 T1057
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Sysadmin troubleshooting a failed domain join and opening NetSetup.log with type/notepad/findstr
  • Endpoint management or Autopilot/Intune domain-join diagnostics collecting the file
  • Support tooling (MSDT, SysInternals) bundling NetSetup.log into a diagnostic archive
  • Backup/DLP agent indexing C:\Windows\debug during a scan
  • SCCM/Configuration-Manager join-status collection scripts
Suppression filter
| where InitiatingProcessFileName !in~ ("mmc.exe","msdt.exe","cmdiag.exe") and not (InitiatingProcessFileName =~ "notepad.exe" and InitiatingProcessAccountName has "admin")
Response runbook
Step 1 (triage): Identify the process reading NetSetup.log — is it a legit admin tool (notepad/findstr run by a known admin) or an unknown/side-loaded DLL host? Correlate with any unbcl.dll side-load on the same host in the prior hours. Step 2 (contain): If the accessing process is unattributed or matches the side-load host, isolate the endpoint and capture memory before killing the process. Step 3 (hunt): Look for accompanying process-list enumeration, screenshot capture, and outbound HTTPS beaconing (NightLedger C2); pivot to other domain hosts for the same file-access pattern to scope lateral spread.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where ProcessCommandLine has "NetSetup.log"
| where AccountName !endswith "$"
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, FileName, ProcessCommandLine,
          InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessFolderPath
| order by Timestamp desc
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where EventID == 4688
| where CommandLine has "NetSetup.log"
| where SubjectUserName !endswith "$"
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, SubjectUserName, NewProcessName, CommandLine, ParentProcessName
| order by TimeGenerated desc

C2 channel detection via inter-beacon-time stddev / fan-out to single dest.
ATT&CKT1071.001 T1071.004
Data sourcesNetwork_Traffic.All_Traffic DeviceNetworkEvents
DeviceNetworkEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(1d)
| where RemoteIPType == "Public" and ActionType == "ConnectionSuccess"
| project DeviceName, RemoteIP, RemotePort, Timestamp

Phishing-link click correlated to endpoint execution Delivery High
User received an external email containing a URL, clicked it, and within 60 seconds the recipient's endpoint spawned a scripting interpreter or network downloader (PowerShell / cmd / mshta / curl / certutil / bitsadmin). This is the high-fidelity shape — a raw "user clicked an emailed URL" query is too noisy to alert on because every Microsoft 365 tenant generates thousands of legitimate clicks per day. The exec-correlation step suppresses the noise to roughly the rate at which a click actually drives onto-host execution, which is the actionable signal. Pair with UC_PHISH_LINK_BYPASS (Safe Links override) and UC_PHISH_LINK_NEWDOMAIN for orthogonal high-fidelity variants.
ATT&CKT1566.002 T1204.001 T1059.001
Data sourcesEmail.All_Email Web Endpoint.Processes EmailEvents EmailUrlInfo UrlClickEvents DeviceProcessEvents
// Phishing-link click that drives endpoint execution within 60s.
// Far higher fidelity than "every clicked URL" — most legitimate clicks
// never spawn a non-browser child process, so the join eliminates the
// 99% of noise that makes a raw click query unactionable.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let SuspectClicks = UrlClickEvents
    | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where AccountName !endswith "$"
    | where ActionType in ("ClickAllowed","ClickedThrough")
    | join kind=inner (
        EmailEvents
        | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
        | where DeliveryAction == "Delivered"
        | where EmailDirection == "Inbound"
        | project NetworkMessageId, Subject, SenderFromAddress, SenderFromDomain,
                  RecipientEmailAddress, EmailTimestamp = Timestamp
      ) on NetworkMessageId
    | join kind=leftouter (
        EmailUrlInfo | project NetworkMessageId, Url, UrlDomain
      ) on NetworkMessageId, Url
    | project ClickTime = Timestamp, AccountUpn, IPAddress, Url, UrlDomain,
              Subject, SenderFromAddress, SenderFromDomain, RecipientEmailAddress,
              ActionType;
// Correlate to a non-browser child process spawned within 60 seconds on
// the recipient's device.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe",
                                         "outlook.exe","brave.exe","arc.exe")
| where FileName in~ ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","cmd.exe","mshta.exe",
                        "rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe",
                        "bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe","curl.exe","wget.exe")
| join kind=inner SuspectClicks on $left.AccountName == $right.AccountUpn
| where Timestamp between (ClickTime .. ClickTime + 60s)
| project ClickTime, ProcessTime = Timestamp,
          DelaySec = datetime_diff('second', Timestamp, ClickTime),
          DeviceName, AccountName, RecipientEmailAddress, SenderFromAddress,
          Subject, Url, UrlDomain, ActionType,
          FileName, ProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessFileName
| order by ClickTime desc
// UrlClickEvents has no clean Sentinel-native equivalent. The detection
// pivots to: Office Send→Receive proximity to SecurityEvent 4688 of a
// non-browser child process. Lower fidelity than the Defender version.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let SuspectMailUsers = OfficeActivity
    | where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where OfficeWorkload == "Exchange"
    | where Operation =~ "Receive"
    | summarize Subject = any(Subject), Sender = any(Sender)
                by MailboxOwnerUPN, MessageId, EmailTime = bin(TimeGenerated, 1m);
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
| where EventID == 4688
| where ParentProcessName has_any ("\chrome.exe","\msedge.exe",
                                     "\firefox.exe","\outlook.exe","\brave.exe")
| where NewProcessName has_any ("\powershell.exe","\pwsh.exe","\cmd.exe",
                                  "\mshta.exe","\rundll32.exe","\regsvr32.exe",
                                  "\wscript.exe","\cscript.exe","\bitsadmin.exe",
                                  "\certutil.exe","\curl.exe","\wget.exe")
| join kind=inner SuspectMailUsers on $left.Account == $right.MailboxOwnerUPN
| where TimeGenerated between (EmailTime .. EmailTime + 60s)
| project TimeGenerated, EmailTime, Computer, Account, ParentProcessName,
          NewProcessName, CommandLine, Sender, Subject
| order by TimeGenerated desc

Trojanized MeshAgent installed as SYSTEM auto-start service (Sinobi backdoor) AIInstallation High
Hunts the Sinobi ransomware crew's covert C2: a weaponized open-source MeshAgent (MeshCentral) binary launched by the Service Control Manager as an NT AUTHORITY\SYSTEM auto-start service. Article-specific because it pairs the MeshAgent product/binary identity with a services.exe parent and SYSTEM integrity, not a generic RMM-install alert. Rationale: Anchors on the article's exact tradecraft — MeshAgent 'installed as a SYSTEM-level auto-start service' as Sinobi's primary C2 — by requiring the services.exe parent + SYSTEM integrity + MeshAgent product identity together, which legitimate ad-hoc RMM use rarely satisfies. Cross-checked against: • https://blog.talosintelligence.com/ir-trends-q2-2026/ • https://blackpointcyber.com/threat-profile/sinobi-ransomware/ • https://socradar.io/blog/dark-web-profile-sinobi-ransomware/ • https://www.microsoft.com/en-us/wdsi/threats/malware-encyclopedia-description?Name=Trojan%3AWin32%2FMeshAgent%21MSR
ATT&CKT1543.003 T1219
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Legitimate MeshCentral/MeshAgent deployment by IT for endpoint management (runs as SYSTEM service by design)
  • MSP-managed hosts where MeshCentral is the sanctioned RMM
  • Security team red-team or purple-team exercises deploying MeshAgent
  • Re-installation/upgrade of an approved MeshCentral agent triggering a fresh 7045
Suppression filter
| where FolderPath !startswith @"C:\Program Files\Mesh Agent\" and FolderPath !startswith @"C:\Program Files\MeshCentral\"
Response runbook
1) Triage: confirm the MeshAgent SHA256 and its C2 endpoint against your approved RMM inventory; pull the service config path and the WSS server it connects to. If the server is not your MeshCentral instance, treat as malicious. 2) Contain: isolate the host, stop and delete the service, and block the C2 FQDN/IP at the proxy/firewall fleet-wide. 3) Hunt: sweep for the same MeshAgent hash/service name across the domain, review RDP/WinRM logons from the same account, and check for ntds.dit access and rclone staging — Sinobi dwells ~3 days before encryption.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName =~ "services.exe"          // launched by Service Control Manager
| where FileName has "meshagent"
    or ProcessVersionInfoProductName has "MeshCentral"
    or ProcessVersionInfoInternalFileName has "MeshAgent"
    or ProcessVersionInfoOriginalFileName has "MeshAgent"
| where ProcessIntegrityLevel in ("System","system")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, FileName, FolderPath, SHA256,
          ProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessFileName, ProcessIntegrityLevel,
          ProcessVersionInfoProductName
| order by Timestamp desc
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where EventID in (4697, 7045)                              // 4697 Security / 7045 System service install
| where ServiceFileName has "meshagent" or ServiceName has "Mesh"
| where isempty(ServiceStartType) or ServiceStartType has "Auto"   // auto-start persistence
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, InstalledBy = SubjectUserName,
          ServiceName, ServiceFileName, ServiceStartType, ServiceAccount, ServiceType
| order by TimeGenerated desc
title: MeshAgent Weaponized as SYSTEM Service by Service Control Manager
id: 8f3c1a92-2d47-4b0e-9a11-5c7d0e2f4a10
description: Detects a MeshAgent/MeshCentral binary spawned by services.exe at SYSTEM integrity, matching Sinobi ransomware covert backdoor tradecraft.
references:
  - https://blog.talosintelligence.com/ir-trends-q2-2026/
author: SOC Detection Engineering
date: 2026/07/28
tags:

  - attack.t1219
logsource:

  product: windows
detection:
  parent:
    ParentImage|endswith: '\services.exe'
  agent:
    - Image|contains: 'meshagent'
    - Product|contains: 'MeshCentral'
    - OriginalFileName: 'MeshAgent.exe'
  integrity:
    IntegrityLevel:
      - 'System'
      - 'S-1-16-16384'
  condition: parent and agent and integrity
level: high
source:windows.sysmon @EventID:1 @ParentImage:(*\services.exe OR *\Services.exe) (@Image:(*\MeshAgent.exe OR *\meshagent.exe OR *\MeshAgent64.exe OR *\MESHAGENT.EXE) OR @Product:(*MeshCentral* OR *meshcentral*))
#event_simpleName=ProcessRollup2 ParentBaseFileName=/services\.exe/i
| ImageFileName=/meshagent/i
| IntegrityLevel=/System/i
| groupBy([aid, ComputerName, ImageFileName, CommandLine, SHA256HashData], function=count())

| `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)`

Sinobi/ARToken attacker-infrastructure callbacks (pamconj.com C2 domains) AICommand & Control High
Detects any host resolving or connecting to the named UAT-11764/ARToken/Sinobi infrastructure dashboard-bl.pamconj.com and spx.pamconj.com, or a MeshAgent process beaconing outbound over 443/WSS. High-fidelity because the domains are concrete IOCs and the MeshAgent-to-internet clause pins the C2 to a process the article names. Rationale: Uses the pre-extracted attacker domains (dashboard-bl.pamconj.com, spx.pamconj.com) as direct IOCs and folds in the article's MeshAgent-over-WSS behaviour so the network side stays process-attributed rather than a bare domain block. Cross-checked against: • https://blog.talosintelligence.com/ir-trends-q2-2026/ • https://blog.talosintelligence.com/artoken-inside-an-eviltokens-affiliate-panel-targeting-microsoft-365/
ATT&CKT1219 T1071.001
Data sourcesNetwork_Resolution.DNS
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Security researcher or TI-enrichment sandbox resolving the IOC domains during analysis
  • Proxy/DNS-logging appliance replaying blocklisted domains for validation
  • Threat-intel platform performing scheduled domain reputation lookups from a scanning host
  • Legitimate but unrelated future re-registration of pamconj.com after takedown
Response runbook
1) Triage: identify the resolving host and the process that initiated the query (ContextImageFileName / InitiatingProcessFileName). A MeshAgent or unknown binary as the source confirms C2. 2) Contain: sinkhole/block *.pamconj.com at DNS and egress proxy; isolate the source host. 3) Hunt: pivot on the resolved IP for other internal clients, correlate with MeshAgent service installs (UC1) and RDP/WinRM lateral movement, and check for device-code sign-ins from the same user set.
let C2Domains = dynamic(["dashboard-bl.pamconj.com","spx.pamconj.com"]);
DeviceNetworkEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where RemoteUrl in~ (C2Domains)
    or (RemoteUrl has "pamconj.com")
    or (InitiatingProcessFileName has "meshagent" and RemotePort in (443, 4433) and RemoteIPType == "Public")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine,
          RemoteUrl, RemoteIP, RemotePort, InitiatingProcessAccountName
| order by Timestamp desc
DnsEvents
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where Name has "pamconj.com"
| where Name in~ ("dashboard-bl.pamconj.com","spx.pamconj.com") or Name endswith ".pamconj.com"
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, ClientIP, Name, QueryTypeName, ResultCodeName, IPAddresses = Result
| order by TimeGenerated desc

Warlock (Storm-2603) Zoho Assist Unattended Agent deployment AIInstallation Medium
Hunts installation/execution of the Zoho Assist Unattended Agent that Warlock/Storm-2603 dropped for headless, sessionless remote control. Article-specific: keys on Zoho Assist unattended-agent binaries/service install rather than any generic RMM. Rationale: Targets the article's named tool — 'Zoho Assist Unattended Agent' deployed by Warlock/Storm-2603 for sessionless remote control — by matching Zoho Assist agent binaries + unattended/install flags, corroborated by ReliaQuest and TheHackerNews reporting on Storm-2603's Zoho Assist use. Cross-checked against: • https://blog.talosintelligence.com/ir-trends-q2-2026/ • https://reliaquest.com/blog/threat-spotlight-storm-2603-exploits-CVE-2026-23760-to-stage-warlock-ransomware/ • https://cybersecuritynews.com/hackers-use-velociraptor-cloudflare-tunnels-zoho-assist/ • https://www.fortiguard.com/threat-actor/6192/storm-2603
ATT&CKT1219 T1543.003
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Helpdesk/MSP that legitimately uses Zoho Assist for unattended support
  • Sanctioned Zoho Assist upgrade or reinstall by IT
  • End user installing Zoho Assist for personal remote-support use
  • Software-deployment tooling (SCCM/Intune) rolling out an approved Zoho package
Suppression filter
| where not (InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("ccmexec.exe","intunemanagementextension.exe") and AccountName endswith "$")
Response runbook
1) Triage: confirm whether Zoho Assist is an approved RMM in the org and whether this host/user is authorized; check the installing account and parent process. 2) Contain: if unauthorized, uninstall the unattended agent, revoke the Zoho device token, isolate the host, and block Zoho Assist relay domains at egress. 3) Hunt: look for co-deployed persistence (Cloudflare tunnels, VS Code SSH, Velociraptor) that Storm-2603 chains for redundancy, and review SharePoint-facing servers for the initial exploitation vector.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where FileName has_any ("ZohoURS","ZMAgent","ZohoMeeting","ZA_Access","ZA_Connect","Zaservice")
    or ProcessVersionInfoCompanyName has "ZOHO"
    or ProcessCommandLine has "Zoho Assist"
| where ProcessCommandLine has_any ("Unattended","install","/silent","-silent","/S")
    or InitiatingProcessFileName =~ "services.exe"
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, FileName, FolderPath, SHA256,
          ProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessFileName, ProcessVersionInfoCompanyName
| order by Timestamp desc
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where EventID == 4688
| where NewProcessName has_any ("ZohoURS","ZMAgent","ZohoMeeting","ZA_Access","ZA_Connect")
    or CommandLine has "Zoho Assist"
| where CommandLine has_any ("Unattended","install","silent") or ParentProcessName has "services.exe"
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, SubjectUserName, NewProcessName, CommandLine, ParentProcessName
| order by TimeGenerated desc
title: Zoho Assist Unattended Agent Installation

rclone.exe cloud-exfiltration staging (Sinobi pre-ransom double-extortion) AIActions on Objectives High
Detects rclone (native or renamed) executing copy/sync/move to a remote backend with config/transfer flags — the data-staging step observed before Sinobi encryption. Article-specific to the named rclone.exe exfil-staging behaviour, using original-file-name matching to survive renaming. Rationale: Directly hunts the article's stated 'data exfiltration staging activity conducted via rclone.exe'; the verb+flag combination and OriginalFileName match make it robust to renaming while staying far above benign rclone use. Cross-checked against: • https://blog.talosintelligence.com/ir-trends-q2-2026/ • https://www.attackiq.com/2026/04/02/sinobi-ransomware/
ATT&CKT1567.002 T1020
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Backup/DevOps engineer legitimately using rclone to sync to S3/B2/cloud storage
  • Automated backup job invoking rclone with a config file
  • Cloud-migration project moving file shares via rclone
  • Personal use of rclone by a power user for their own cloud drive
Suppression filter
| where not (InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("veeam.backup.manager.exe","restic.exe") or FolderPath has @"\Backup\")
Response runbook
1) Triage: read the full command line for the remote backend and source path — identify what data set was targeted and whether the destination is a sanctioned corporate cloud account. 2) Contain: kill the process, block the remote backend endpoint at egress, and preserve the rclone config file (holds the exfil destination/creds). 3) Hunt: on the same host/account look for MeshAgent C2, ntds.dit access, and impending encryption; measure outbound byte volume to gauge exfil scope and trigger data-breach IR if confirmed.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where FileName =~ "rclone.exe" or ProcessVersionInfoOriginalFileName =~ "rclone.exe" or ProcessVersionInfoProductName has "rclone"
| where ProcessCommandLine has_any (" copy"," sync"," move"," lsjson")
| where ProcessCommandLine has_any ("--config","--transfers","--multi-thread-streams","--no-check-certificate","--ignore-existing","--drive-","mega:","b2:","s3:")
| where AccountName !endswith "$"
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, FileName, FolderPath, SHA256,
          ProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessFileName
| order by Timestamp desc
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where EventID == 4688
| where NewProcessName endswith "\\rclone.exe" or CommandLine has "rclone"
| where CommandLine has_any (" copy"," sync"," move")
| where CommandLine has_any ("--config","--transfers","--multi-thread-streams","--no-check-certificate","mega:","b2:","s3:")
| where AccountName !endswith "$"
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, SubjectUserName, NewProcessName, CommandLine, ParentProcessName
| order by TimeGenerated desc
title: Rclone Cloud Exfiltration Command Line

Mass file rename to .SINOBI extension (ransomware encryption in progress) AIActions on Objectives High
Fires when a single host/process writes or renames files to the .SINOBI extension above a burst threshold — the encryption stage of a Sinobi ransomware event. Article-specific via the concrete .SINOBI extension and a per-host volume threshold to distinguish encryption from stray files. Rationale: The '.SINOBI file extension' is a concrete, article-named encryption artefact; a per-host burst threshold (>50) turns individual noisy file events into a single high-severity ransomware-in-progress alert. Cross-checked against: • https://blog.talosintelligence.com/ir-trends-q2-2026/ • https://www.ransomware.live/group/sinobi • https://www.moxfive.com/resources/moxfive-threat-actor-spotlight-sinobi
ATT&CKT1486
Data sourcesEndpoint.Filesystem
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • A security analyst intentionally handling recovered .SINOBI samples in a lab share
  • Backup restore replaying previously-encrypted .SINOBI files onto a host
  • Malware researcher bulk-copying an IOC set that includes .SINOBI-named files
  • EDR quarantine/rehydration moving encrypted artefacts (usually below threshold)
Response runbook
1) Triage: confirm the InitiatingProcess writing .SINOBI files and the affected share/host — this is likely already active encryption. 2) Contain: immediately isolate the host, kill the encrypting process, disable the deploying account, and check for a malicious GPO logon script pushing encryption domain-wide (block/remove it before it fans out). 3) Hunt: identify patient-zero and the MeshAgent C2 dwell window, quantify encrypted scope, verify offline backups, and preserve rclone exfil evidence for breach notification.
DeviceFileEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where ActionType in ("FileRenamed","FileCreated","FileModified")
| where FileName endswith ".SINOBI" or PreviousFileName endswith ".SINOBI"
| summarize FileCount = count(), FirstSeen = min(Timestamp), LastSeen = max(Timestamp),
            SampleFile = any(FolderPath)
            by DeviceName, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessSHA256
| where FileCount > 50           // burst threshold: mass encryption, not a stray file
| order by FileCount desc
ImFileEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where TargetFileName endswith ".SINOBI" or TargetFileExtension =~ "SINOBI"
| summarize FileCount = count(), FirstSeen = min(TimeGenerated), LastSeen = max(TimeGenerated),
            SampleFile = any(TargetFilePath), Proc = any(ActingProcessName)
            by DvcHostname
| where FileCount > 50
| order by FileCount desc
title: File Written With .SINOBI Ransomware Extension
id: 3c8e2f4a-6b19-4a70-9d52-1e7b0c5a2f91

OAuth device-code authentication flow sign-in (ARToken/EvilTokens MFA bypass) AIDelivery Medium
Surfaces successful Azure AD/Entra sign-ins completed through the OAuth device authorization flow — the MFA-bypass primitive the ARToken PhaaS panel weaponizes to issue tokens to the attacker instead of stealing passwords. Article-specific to the device-code + PRT abuse, not generic risky-sign-in scoring. Rationale: Pins the ARToken/EvilTokens core technique — 'bypass MFA through the OAuth device authorization flow rather than stealing passwords' — to the device-code sign-in signal; corroborated by the Talos ARToken deep-dive and BleepingComputer/gbhackers reporting. Datadog/Falcon/CloudWatch left empty: this depends on Entra SignInLogs not shipped to those platforms in this tenant. Cross-checked against: • https://blog.talosintelligence.com/ir-trends-q2-2026/ • https://blog.talosintelligence.com/artoken-inside-an-eviltokens-affiliate-panel-targeting-microsoft-365/ • https://www.bleepingcomputer.com/news/security/artoken-phaas-exposes-eviltokens-microsoft-365-phishing-toolkit/ • https://gbhackers.com/eviltokens-linked-artoken-panel/
ATT&CKT1550.001 T1566.002
Data sourcesAuthentication
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Legitimate device-code sign-in on input-constrained devices (smart TVs, conference-room/IoT, CLI tools like Azure CLI 'az login --use-device-code')
  • Developers authenticating headless services or automation via device code
  • PowerShell/Graph SDK interactive device-code auth by admins
  • New device onboarding flows that legitimately use device code
Suppression filter
| where not (AppDisplayName in ("Microsoft Azure CLI","Microsoft Azure PowerShell") and DeviceTrustType == "Azure AD joined")
Response runbook
1) Triage: correlate the device-code sign-in's IP/geo/ASN and target resource against the user's baseline; a mismatch between the user's location and the authenticating device strongly indicates phishing. 2) Contain: revoke the user's refresh tokens/sessions, force re-auth, remove any newly-registered MFA methods or self-enrolled devices, and hunt for a fresh PRT. 3) Hunt: review the mailbox for attacker inbox rules, SharePoint/OneDrive bulk access, and internal phishing sent from the account; apply Conditional Access blocking device-code flow for the affected population.
AADSignInEventsBeta
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| extend ProcDetails = tostring(AuthenticationProcessingDetails)
| where ProcDetails has "Device Code" or ProcDetails has "deviceCode"
| where ErrorCode == 0                                    // successful token issuance
| project Timestamp, AccountUpn, Application, ApplicationId, IPAddress, Country, City,
          ClientAppUsed, DeviceTrustType, ResourceDisplayName, ProcDetails
| order by Timestamp desc
SigninLogs
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| extend ProcDetails = tostring(AuthenticationProcessingDetails)
// SigninLogs schema here has no AuthenticationProtocol column; device-code flow is
// identified via the processing-details blob instead.
| where ProcDetails has "Device Code" or ProcDetails has "deviceCode"
| where ResultType == 0
| project TimeGenerated, UserPrincipalName, AppDisplayName, AppId, IPAddress, Location,
          ClientAppUsed, ResourceDisplayName, ConditionalAccessStatus, ProcDetails
| order by TimeGenerated desc
title: Azure AD OAuth Device Code Flow Sign-In

UAT-11764 QR-phishing credential-harvesting host (workers.dev) click/callback AIDelivery High
Detects Safe Links clicks and host DNS/network callbacks to the named UAT-11764 M365 credential-harvesting page clear90489058903-document.workers.dev, delivered via QR codes in PDF attachments. Article-specific via the concrete harvesting FQDN. Rationale: Uses the pre-extracted harvesting FQDN clear90489058903-document.workers.dev as a direct IOC; leads with UrlClickEvents so a Safe Links click-through (not just delivery) is captured, which is the highest-fidelity signal that a QR-PDF recipient reached the credential page. Cross-checked against: • https://blog.talosintelligence.com/ir-trends-q2-2026/
ATT&CKT1566.002 T1598.003
Data sourcesNetwork_Resolution.DNS
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Security awareness team detonating the phishing URL in a sandbox for analysis
  • SOC analyst manually visiting the reported IOC during triage
  • URL-detonation/enrichment appliance auto-fetching the domain
  • Takedown/registrar validation traffic to the host
Response runbook
1) Triage: identify who clicked (AccountUpn) and whether IsClickedThrough is true; check the same user's subsequent Entra sign-ins for a device-code grant or AiTM token issuance. 2) Contain: revoke sessions/tokens for any user who reached the page, force password reset + MFA re-registration, and block the workers.dev host at proxy/DNS. 3) Hunt: search EmailEvents/EmailAttachmentInfo for the PDF lures across the org, look for attacker inbox rules and SharePoint-hosted lure docs, and identify internal senders propagating the campaign from compromised mailbox contact lists.
UrlClickEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where Url has "clear90489058903-document.workers.dev"
| project Timestamp, AccountUpn, Url, ActionType, IsClickedThrough, IPAddress, Workload, DetectionMethods
| order by Timestamp desc
DnsEvents
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where Name =~ "clear90489058903-document.workers.dev"
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, ClientIP, Name, QueryTypeName, ResultCodeName, IPAddresses = Result
| order by TimeGenerated desc
title: DNS Query to UAT-11764 workers.dev Credential-Harvesting Host

C2 channel detection via inter-beacon-time stddev / fan-out to single dest.
ATT&CKT1071.001 T1071.004
Data sourcesNetwork_Traffic.All_Traffic DeviceNetworkEvents
DeviceNetworkEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(1d)
| where RemoteIPType == "Public" and ActionType == "ConnectionSuccess"
| project DeviceName, RemoteIP, RemotePort, Timestamp

| extend prev_dev = prev(DeviceName, 1), prev_ip = prev(RemoteIP, 1),
         prev_port = prev(RemotePort, 1), prev_ts = prev(Timestamp, 1)
| where DeviceName == prev_dev and RemoteIP == prev_ip and RemotePort == prev_port
| extend delta_sec = datetime_diff('second', Timestamp, prev_ts)
| summarize conn_count = count(), avg_delta = avg(delta_sec), stdev_delta = stdev(delta_sec)
    by DeviceName, RemoteIP, RemotePort
| where conn_count > 30 and avg_delta between (30.0 .. 600.0) and stdev_delta < 5.0
| order by conn_count desc
ImNetworkSession
| where TimeGenerated > ago(2h)
| where DvcAction != "Block"
| where ipv4_is_private(DstIpAddr) == false
| summarize ConnCount = count(),
            DistinctMinutes = dcount(bin(TimeGenerated, 1m))
            by DvcHostname, DstIpAddr, DstPortNumber
| where ConnCount > 50 and DistinctMinutes > 30   // sustained, not bursty
| order by ConnCount desc

Phishing-link click correlated to endpoint execution Delivery High
User received an external email containing a URL, clicked it, and within 60 seconds the recipient's endpoint spawned a scripting interpreter or network downloader (PowerShell / cmd / mshta / curl / certutil / bitsadmin). This is the high-fidelity shape — a raw "user clicked an emailed URL" query is too noisy to alert on because every Microsoft 365 tenant generates thousands of legitimate clicks per day. The exec-correlation step suppresses the noise to roughly the rate at which a click actually drives onto-host execution, which is the actionable signal. Pair with UC_PHISH_LINK_BYPASS (Safe Links override) and UC_PHISH_LINK_NEWDOMAIN for orthogonal high-fidelity variants.
ATT&CKT1566.002 T1204.001 T1059.001
Data sourcesEmail.All_Email Web Endpoint.Processes EmailEvents EmailUrlInfo UrlClickEvents DeviceProcessEvents
// Phishing-link click that drives endpoint execution within 60s.
// Far higher fidelity than "every clicked URL" — most legitimate clicks
// never spawn a non-browser child process, so the join eliminates the
// 99% of noise that makes a raw click query unactionable.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let SuspectClicks = UrlClickEvents
    | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where AccountName !endswith "$"
    | where ActionType in ("ClickAllowed","ClickedThrough")
    | join kind=inner (
        EmailEvents
        | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
        | where DeliveryAction == "Delivered"
        | where EmailDirection == "Inbound"
        | project NetworkMessageId, Subject, SenderFromAddress, SenderFromDomain,
                  RecipientEmailAddress, EmailTimestamp = Timestamp
      ) on NetworkMessageId
    | join kind=leftouter (
        EmailUrlInfo | project NetworkMessageId, Url, UrlDomain
      ) on NetworkMessageId, Url
    | project ClickTime = Timestamp, AccountUpn, IPAddress, Url, UrlDomain,
              Subject, SenderFromAddress, SenderFromDomain, RecipientEmailAddress,
              ActionType;
// Correlate to a non-browser child process spawned within 60 seconds on
// the recipient's device.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe",
                                         "outlook.exe","brave.exe","arc.exe")
| where FileName in~ ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","cmd.exe","mshta.exe",
                        "rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe",
                        "bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe","curl.exe","wget.exe")
| join kind=inner SuspectClicks on $left.AccountName == $right.AccountUpn
| where Timestamp between (ClickTime .. ClickTime + 60s)
| project ClickTime, ProcessTime = Timestamp,
          DelaySec = datetime_diff('second', Timestamp, ClickTime),
          DeviceName, AccountName, RecipientEmailAddress, SenderFromAddress,
          Subject, Url, UrlDomain, ActionType,
          FileName, ProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessFileName
| order by ClickTime desc
// UrlClickEvents has no clean Sentinel-native equivalent. The detection
// pivots to: Office Send→Receive proximity to SecurityEvent 4688 of a
// non-browser child process. Lower fidelity than the Defender version.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let SuspectMailUsers = OfficeActivity
    | where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where OfficeWorkload == "Exchange"
    | where Operation =~ "Receive"
    | summarize Subject = any(Subject), Sender = any(Sender)
                by MailboxOwnerUPN, MessageId, EmailTime = bin(TimeGenerated, 1m);
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
| where EventID == 4688
| where ParentProcessName has_any ("\chrome.exe","\msedge.exe",
                                     "\firefox.exe","\outlook.exe","\brave.exe")
| where NewProcessName has_any ("\powershell.exe","\pwsh.exe","\cmd.exe",
                                  "\mshta.exe","\rundll32.exe","\regsvr32.exe",
                                  "\wscript.exe","\cscript.exe","\bitsadmin.exe",
                                  "\certutil.exe","\curl.exe","\wget.exe")
| join kind=inner SuspectMailUsers on $left.Account == $right.MailboxOwnerUPN
| where TimeGenerated between (EmailTime .. EmailTime + 60s)
| project TimeGenerated, EmailTime, Computer, Account, ParentProcessName,
          NewProcessName, CommandLine, Sender, Subject
| order by TimeGenerated desc
WEB
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
``` Phishing-link click that drives endpoint execution within 60s ```
| tstats `summariesonly` earliest(_time) AS click_time
    from datamodel=Web
    where Web.action="allowed"
    by Web.src, Web.user, Web.dest, Web.url
| `drop_dm_object_name(Web)`
| rename user AS recipient, dest AS clicked_domain, url AS clicked_url
| join type=inner recipient
    [| tstats `summariesonly` count
         from datamodel=Email.All_Email
         where All_Email.action="delivered" AND All_Email.url!="-"
         by All_Email.recipient, All_Email.src_user, All_Email.url, All_Email.subject
     | `drop_dm_object_name(All_Email)`
     | rex field=url "https?://(?<email_domain>[^/]+)"
     | rename recipient AS recipient]
| join type=inner src
    [| tstats `summariesonly` earliest(_time) AS exec_time
         values(Processes.process) AS exec_cmd, values(Processes.process_name) AS exec_proc
         from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
         where Processes.parent_process_name IN ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe",
                                                   "outlook.exe","brave.exe","arc.exe")
           AND Processes.process_name IN ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","cmd.exe","mshta.exe",
                                            "rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","wscript.exe",
                                            "cscript.exe","bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe",
                                            "curl.exe","wget.exe")
         by Processes.dest, Processes.user
     | `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)`
     | rename dest AS src]
| eval delta_sec = exec_time - click_time
| where delta_sec >= 0 AND delta_sec <= 60
| table click_time, exec_time, delta_sec, recipient, src, src_user, subject,
        clicked_domain, clicked_url, exec_proc, exec_cmd
| sort - click_time
``` Phishing-link click that drives endpoint execution within 60s ```
| tstats summariesonly=false earliest(_time) AS click_time
    from datamodel=Web
    where Web.action="allowed"
    by Web.src, Web.user, Web.dest, Web.url
| `drop_dm_object_name(Web)`

| join type=inner recipient
    [| tstats summariesonly=false count
         from datamodel=Email.All_Email
         where All_Email.action="delivered" AND All_Email.url!="-"
         by All_Email.recipient, All_Email.src_user, All_Email.url, All_Email.subject
     | `drop_dm_object_name(All_Email)`
     | rex field=url "https?://(?<email_domain>[^/]+)"
     | rename recipient AS recipient]
| join type=inner src
    [| tstats summariesonly=false earliest(_time) AS exec_time
         values(Processes.process) AS exec_cmd, values(Processes.process_name) AS exec_proc
         from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
         where Processes.parent_process_name IN ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe",
                                                   "outlook.exe","brave.exe","arc.exe")
           AND Processes.process_name IN ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","cmd.exe","mshta.exe",
                                            "rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","wscript.exe",
                                            "cscript.exe","bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe",
                                            "curl.exe","wget.exe")
         by Processes.dest, Processes.user
     | `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)`
     | rename dest AS src]
| eval delta_sec = exec_time - click_time
| where delta_sec >= 0 AND delta_sec <= 60
| table click_time, exec_time, delta_sec, recipient, src, src_user, subject,
        clicked_domain, clicked_url, exec_proc, exec_cmd
| sort - click_time
Email attachment opened from external sender Delivery High
Attachment delivery + execution by recipient — most common malware initial access.
ATT&CKT1566.001 T1204.002
Data sourcesEmail.All_Email Endpoint.Processes EmailAttachmentInfo DeviceProcessEvents
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let MalAttachments = EmailAttachmentInfo
    | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where AccountName !endswith "$"
    | project NetworkMessageId, RecipientEmailAddress,
              AttachmentFileName = FileName, AttachmentSHA256 = SHA256;
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("OUTLOOK.EXE","winword.exe","excel.exe","powerpnt.exe")
| where FileName in~ ("cmd.exe","powershell.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe",
                      "mshta.exe","rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe")
| join kind=inner MalAttachments on $left.AccountUpn == $right.RecipientEmailAddress
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, FileName, ProcessCommandLine,
          InitiatingProcessFileName, AttachmentFileName, AttachmentSHA256
// Sentinel doesn't have an attachment-hash table. Best approximation:
// OfficeActivity Send/Receive activity + correlate to host process spawn.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let MailWithAttach = OfficeActivity
    | where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where OfficeWorkload == "Exchange"
    | where Operation in~ ("Send","Receive")
    | where isnotempty(MessageId)
    | project EmailTime = TimeGenerated, MailboxOwnerUPN, Sender,
              Recipients, Subject, MessageId;
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
| where EventID == 4688
| where ParentProcessName endswith "OUTLOOK.EXE"
| where NewProcessName endswith "\cmd.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\powershell.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\wscript.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\cscript.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\mshta.exe"
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, Account, NewProcessName, CommandLine,
          ParentProcessName
| order by TimeGenerated desc
ENDPOINT
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
| tstats `summariesonly` count
    from datamodel=Email.All_Email
    where All_Email.file_name!="-"
    by All_Email.src_user, All_Email.recipient, All_Email.file_name, All_Email.subject
| rename All_Email.recipient as user
| join type=inner user
    [| tstats `summariesonly` count
        from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
        where Processes.parent_process_name IN ("OUTLOOK.EXE","winword.exe","excel.exe","powerpnt.exe")
          AND Processes.process_name IN ("cmd.exe","powershell.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe","mshta.exe","rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe")
        by Processes.dest, Processes.user, Processes.parent_process_name, Processes.process_name, Processes.process
     | rename Processes.user as user]
| tstats summariesonly=false count
    from datamodel=Email.All_Email
    where All_Email.file_name!="-"
    by All_Email.src_user, All_Email.recipient, All_Email.file_name, All_Email.subject
| rename All_Email.recipient as user
| join type=inner user
    [| tstats summariesonly=false count
        from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
        where Processes.parent_process_name IN ("OUTLOOK.EXE","winword.exe","excel.exe","powerpnt.exe")
          AND Processes.process_name IN ("cmd.exe","powershell.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe","mshta.exe","rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe")
        by Processes.dest, Processes.user, Processes.parent_process_name, Processes.process_name, Processes.process
     | rename Processes.user as user]

Ransomware-style mass file rename / extension change Actions on Objectives Medium
Threshold detection: many files renamed in short window, often with new extension.
ATT&CKT1486
Data sourcesEndpoint.Filesystem DeviceFileEvents
DeviceFileEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(1d)
| where InitiatingProcessAccountName !endswith "$"
| where ActionType in ("FileRenamed","FileModified")
| summarize files = dcount(FileName) by DeviceName, InitiatingProcessAccountName, bin(Timestamp, 1m)
| where files > 200    // empirical: > 200 unique-file renames in 1m by one account on one host

| where ActorUsername !endswith "$"
| where EventType in ("FileRenamed","FileModified")
| summarize files = dcount(TargetFileName)
            by DvcHostname, ActorUsername, ActingProcessName, bin(TimeGenerated, 1m)
| where files > 200    // P99 of legit bulk-tooling per-minute rename volume
| order by files desc

// Article-specific bespoke detection — IR Trends Q2 2026: Phishing and weaponized remote management tools drive attack
// Hunts the actual binaries / paths / commandline fragments named
// in the article instead of a generic technique-class template.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where (FileName in~ ("rclone.exe"))
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, FileName,
          FolderPath, ProcessCommandLine,
          InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine
| order by Timestamp desc

// File-creation events for the named binaries / paths
DeviceFileEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where ActionType in ("FileCreated","FileModified")
| where (FileName in~ ("rclone.exe"))
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, FolderPath,
          FileName, ActionType, InitiatingProcessFileName,
          InitiatingProcessCommandLine

TeamCity On-Premises vulnerable to CVE-2026-63077 unauthenticated RCE (version exposure) AIExploitation High
Surfaces TeamCity On-Premises hosts still exposed to CVE-2026-63077, the CVSS 9.8 unauthenticated deserialization RCE in the agent polling protocol. Hunts assets not yet on the fixed builds 2025.11.7 or 2026.1.3 so they can be prioritised for patching or network isolation. Rationale: Uses the concrete CVE-2026-63077 identifier and JetBrains' named fixed builds (2025.11.7 / 2026.1.3). Cross-checked against the JetBrains advisory and IONIX threat page which both confirm 'all TeamCity On-Premises versions' are affected and the CWE-502 agent-polling vector. Cross-checked against: • https://blog.jetbrains.com/teamcity/2026/07/cve-2026-63077/ • https://www.ionix.io/threat-center/cve-2026-63077/
ATT&CKT1190
Data sourcesVulnerabilities.Vulnerabilities
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Host already patched but TVM scan snapshot is stale (scanner has not re-run since update)
  • Decommissioned/offline TeamCity test server that no longer serves traffic
  • Software inventory mis-attributes a bundled TeamCity plugin version to the server product
  • Air-gapped TeamCity instance where the CVE is not reachable over HTTP(S)
Response runbook
Step 1 (triage): Confirm the reported SoftwareVersion is below 2025.11.7 (or below 2026.1.3 on the 2026 branch) and check DeviceInfo.IsInternetFacing/PublicIP to gauge exposure of the agent polling port. Step 2 (contain): For internet-facing instances, place the TeamCity server behind VPN/ACL restricting the agent polling protocol to trusted agent IPs, or apply JetBrains' security-patch plugin (2017.1+) if a full upgrade is blocked. Step 3 (hunt): Pivot to the process/network/file UCs below on the same DeviceId to rule out prior exploitation before the version was flagged.
DeviceTvmSoftwareVulnerabilities
| where Timestamp > ago(1d)
| where CveId == "CVE-2026-63077"
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, DeviceId, SoftwareVendor, SoftwareName, SoftwareVersion, CveId, VulnerabilitySeverityLevel, RecommendedSecurityUpdate
| join kind=leftouter (DeviceInfo | where Timestamp > ago(1d) | summarize arg_max(Timestamp, IsInternetFacing, PublicIP) by DeviceId) on DeviceId
| order by IsInternetFacing desc, Timestamp desc
DeviceTvmSoftwareVulnerabilities
| where TimeGenerated > ago(1d)
| where CveId == "CVE-2026-63077"
| project TimeGenerated, DeviceName, DeviceId, SoftwareVendor, SoftwareName, SoftwareVersion, CveId, VulnerabilitySeverityLevel, RecommendedSecurityUpdate
| order by TimeGenerated desc

| tstats `summariesonly` count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime from datamodel=Vulnerabilities.Vulnerabilities where Vulnerabilities.cve="CVE-2026-63077" by Vulnerabilities.dest, Vulnerabilities.signature, Vulnerabilities.severity, Vulnerabilities.cve
| `drop_dm_object_name(Vulnerabilities)`
| convert ctime(firstTime) ctime(lastTime)

| `drop_dm_object_name(Vulnerabilities)`

TeamCity server process spawns OS command interpreter (CVE-2026-63077 RCE outcome) AIInstallation High
Detects the TeamCity server JVM (or its Windows service wrapper) spawning a command interpreter or discovery binary — the direct outcome of the CVE-2026-63077 deserialization RCE that lets an unauthenticated attacker 'run OS commands' as the server process. Build agents (which legitimately run shells) are explicitly excluded so only anomalous server-side execution surfaces. Rationale: Anchors on the article's core claim ('Run OS Commands' as the TeamCity server process). The parent = TeamCity server JVM / service wrapper with a 'teamcity'/'buildServer.serverSide' signature, explicitly excluding buildAgent so legitimate build-step shells don't fire — the server itself never runs interactive shells in normal operation. Cross-checked against: • https://blog.jetbrains.com/teamcity/2026/07/cve-2026-63077/ • https://www.ionix.io/threat-center/cve-2026-63077/
ATT&CKT1190 T1059.003 T1059.001
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Admin using a TeamCity server-side maintenance script that shells out (e.g. backup/restore wrapper)
  • Server-side build-feature or diagnostics plugin that legitimately invokes net.exe/whoami during startup
  • Monitoring agent mis-attributed as a child of the TeamCity JVM due to process re-parenting
  • A build configuration mistakenly running on the server host rather than a dedicated agent
Suppression filter
| where not (ProcessCommandLine has_any ("\\TeamCity\\backup", "maintainDB", "teamcity-server.bat"))
Response runbook
Step 1 (triage): Pull the full parent JVM command line and the child ChildCmd — legitimate maintenance is usually a known script path; attacker activity shows recon (whoami/net/nltest) or download cradles (certutil/bitsadmin/curl). Correlate the process time against TeamCity server HTTP logs for a preceding agent-polling request. Step 2 (contain): Isolate the host, kill the offending process tree, and rotate any TeamCity-stored service credentials/tokens (the server process holds VCS and deployment secrets). Step 3 (hunt): Run the network-callback and file-drop UCs on the same DeviceId, and check for new admin tokens/users created via the TeamCity REST API.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("java.exe","java","jsvc","TeamCityService.exe","teamcity-server.exe")
| where (InitiatingProcessCommandLine has "teamcity" or InitiatingProcessFolderPath has "TeamCity" or InitiatingProcessCommandLine has "jetbrains.buildServer.serverSide" or InitiatingProcessCommandLine has "BuildServerMain")
| where not (InitiatingProcessCommandLine has "buildAgent" or InitiatingProcessCommandLine has "jetbrains.buildServer.agent")
| where FileName in~ ("cmd.exe","powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe","mshta.exe","rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe","curl.exe","whoami.exe","net.exe","net1.exe","nltest.exe","bash.exe","sh","bash")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, ParentProc = InitiatingProcessFileName, ParentCmd = InitiatingProcessCommandLine, ChildProc = FileName, ChildCmd = ProcessCommandLine, SHA256
| order by Timestamp desc
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where EventID == 4688
| where ParentProcessName has "teamcity" or ParentProcessName has @"\TeamCity\"
| where NewProcessName has_any ("\\cmd.exe","\\powershell.exe","\\pwsh.exe","\\wscript.exe","\\cscript.exe","\\mshta.exe","\\rundll32.exe","\\regsvr32.exe","\\bitsadmin.exe","\\certutil.exe","\\whoami.exe","\\net.exe","\\net1.exe","\\nltest.exe")
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, SubjectUserName, ParentProcessName, NewProcessName, CommandLine
| order by TimeGenerated desc
