Outbound callback from TeamCity-server-spawned interpreter (CVE-2026-63077 reverse shell/C2) AICommand & Control Medium
Flags network connections to public IPs made by command interpreters whose parent is the TeamCity server process — the reverse-shell / C2 stage that follows CVE-2026-63077 RCE. Because the server JVM does not normally spawn shells that then egress, an interpreter-child-of-TeamCity reaching an external host is high-fidelity. Rationale: Ties the article's unauthenticated-RCE outcome to its most likely follow-on (interactive access). Defender's InitiatingProcessParentFileName lets us require the connecting shell be a child of the TeamCity server JVM/service, which is the differentiator from ordinary shell egress. Cross-checked against: • https://blog.jetbrains.com/teamcity/2026/07/cve-2026-63077/ • https://www.ionix.io/threat-center/cve-2026-63077/
ATT&CKT1071.001 T1572
Data sourcesNetwork_Traffic.All_Traffic
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • TeamCity server-side script legitimately using curl/certutil to fetch an internal-then-external artifact
  • PowerShell health-check or plugin update process launched by the server reaching a JetBrains/CDN endpoint
  • Non-TeamCity Java application on the same host whose child shell egresses (java.exe parent name collision)
  • Security tooling injecting a shell under the JVM for scanning
Suppression filter
| where RemotePort !in (443, 80)  // legit server egress is overwhelmingly 80/443; reverse shells cluster on odd ports
Response runbook
Step 1 (triage): Enrich RemoteIP/RemoteUrl against threat intel and WHOIS (newly registered domain, uncommon port such as 4444/1337 = strong). Confirm the parent JVM is the TeamCity server, not another Java app, via the process UC. Step 2 (contain): Block the destination at the egress firewall, isolate the host, and terminate the interpreter process tree. Step 3 (hunt): Sweep other CI/CD hosts for the same RemoteIP/domain, review TeamCity audit log for new tokens/admin users, and check for dropped payloads via the file-write UC.
DeviceNetworkEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where InitiatingProcessParentFileName in~ ("java.exe","jsvc","TeamCityService.exe","teamcity-server.exe")
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("cmd.exe","powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe","bash.exe","sh","nc.exe","ncat.exe","certutil.exe","curl.exe","bitsadmin.exe")
| where RemoteIPType == "Public"
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, InitiatingProcessParentFileName, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, RemoteIP, RemotePort, RemoteUrl
| order by Timestamp desc
// Microsoft Sentinel — auto-derived from the Defender XDR hunt.
// Requires the Microsoft 365 Defender data connector (streams the
// advanced-hunting tables into Sentinel; Timestamp → TimeGenerated).
DeviceNetworkEvents
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where InitiatingProcessParentFileName in~ ("java.exe","jsvc","TeamCityService.exe","teamcity-server.exe")
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("cmd.exe","powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe","bash.exe","sh","nc.exe","ncat.exe","certutil.exe","curl.exe","bitsadmin.exe")
| where RemoteIPType == "Public"
| project TimeGenerated, DeviceName, InitiatingProcessParentFileName, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, RemoteIP, RemotePort, RemoteUrl
| order by TimeGenerated desc
source:windows.sysmon @EventID:3 @Image:(*\\cmd.exe OR *\\CMD.EXE OR *\\powershell.exe OR *\\PowerShell.exe OR *\\POWERSHELL.EXE OR *\\pwsh.exe OR *\\nc.exe OR *\\ncat.exe OR *\\bitsadmin.exe OR *\\certutil.exe OR *\\bash.exe OR *\\TeamCity\\* OR *\\teamcity\\*) -CIDR(@DestinationIp, 10.0.0.0/8) -CIDR(@DestinationIp, 172.16.0.0/12) -CIDR(@DestinationIp, 192.168.0.0/16)

Executable or web-shell written by TeamCity server process (CVE-2026-63077 payload drop) AIInstallation Medium
Detects the TeamCity server JVM writing executables, scripts, or web-shell file types (.exe/.ps1/.bat/.jsp/.php/.aspx/.sh) — tooling or web-shell drops staged after CVE-2026-63077 RCE. The server process legitimately manages .jar/.war/config data, so restricting to script/executable and web-shell extensions keeps this signal high. Rationale: Extends the RCE outcome to tooling/web-shell staging. Anchored on the TeamCity server JVM as writer plus executable/web-shell extensions; .jsp/.php/.aspx dropped by a Java web server strongly implies a web shell, while .exe/.ps1 implies second-stage tooling — neither is normal TeamCity server file activity. Cross-checked against: • https://blog.jetbrains.com/teamcity/2026/07/cve-2026-63077/ • https://www.ionix.io/threat-center/cve-2026-63077/
ATT&CKT1105 T1505.003
Data sourcesEndpoint.Filesystem
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • TeamCity server unpacking a legitimately-installed plugin that ships .ps1/.bat helper scripts into its data directory
  • Server-side auto-update writing a bundled updater .exe
  • Admin manually staging a maintenance script under the TeamCity data dir
  • Backup/export routine writing script templates into the config area
Suppression filter
| where not (FolderPath has "\\plugins\\.unpacked" or FolderPath has "\\temp\\" and FileName endswith ".sh")
Response runbook
Step 1 (triage): Inspect FolderPath — writes into TeamCity webapps/ROOT or plugin web dirs (.jsp/.php/.aspx) are almost certainly web shells; hash the file (SHA256) and detonate/scan. Correlate the write time with a preceding agent-polling HTTP request and the process-spawn UC. Step 2 (contain): Quarantine the file, isolate the host, and preserve it for forensics; rotate TeamCity-stored credentials. Step 3 (hunt): Search web logs for subsequent GET/POST access to the dropped file name, and sweep other CI/CD hosts for the same SHA256.
DeviceFileEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("java.exe","jsvc","TeamCityService.exe","teamcity-server.exe")
| where (InitiatingProcessCommandLine has "teamcity" or InitiatingProcessFolderPath has "TeamCity" or InitiatingProcessCommandLine has "jetbrains.buildServer.serverSide")
| where not (InitiatingProcessCommandLine has "buildAgent" or InitiatingProcessCommandLine has "jetbrains.buildServer.agent")
| where FileName endswith ".exe" or FileName endswith ".ps1" or FileName endswith ".bat" or FileName endswith ".vbs" or FileName endswith ".jsp" or FileName endswith ".php" or FileName endswith ".aspx" or FileName endswith ".sh"
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, FileName, FolderPath, SHA256
| order by Timestamp desc
ImFileEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where EventType == "FileCreated"
| where (ActingProcessName has "java" or ActingProcessName has "teamcity") and (ActingProcessCommandLine has "teamcity" or TargetFilePath has "TeamCity")
| where TargetFileExtension in~ ("exe","ps1","bat","vbs","jsp","php","aspx","sh")
| project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, ActorUsername, ActingProcessName, ActingProcessCommandLine, TargetFilePath, TargetFileName, TargetFileSHA256
| order by TimeGenerated desc

Phishing-link click correlated to endpoint execution Delivery High
User received an external email containing a URL, clicked it, and within 60 seconds the recipient's endpoint spawned a scripting interpreter or network downloader (PowerShell / cmd / mshta / curl / certutil / bitsadmin). This is the high-fidelity shape — a raw "user clicked an emailed URL" query is too noisy to alert on because every Microsoft 365 tenant generates thousands of legitimate clicks per day. The exec-correlation step suppresses the noise to roughly the rate at which a click actually drives onto-host execution, which is the actionable signal. Pair with UC_PHISH_LINK_BYPASS (Safe Links override) and UC_PHISH_LINK_NEWDOMAIN for orthogonal high-fidelity variants.
ATT&CKT1566.002 T1204.001 T1059.001
Data sourcesEmail.All_Email Web Endpoint.Processes EmailEvents EmailUrlInfo UrlClickEvents DeviceProcessEvents
// Phishing-link click that drives endpoint execution within 60s.
// Far higher fidelity than "every clicked URL" — most legitimate clicks
// never spawn a non-browser child process, so the join eliminates the
// 99% of noise that makes a raw click query unactionable.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let SuspectClicks = UrlClickEvents
    | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where AccountName !endswith "$"
    | where ActionType in ("ClickAllowed","ClickedThrough")
    | join kind=inner (
        EmailEvents
        | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
        | where DeliveryAction == "Delivered"
        | where EmailDirection == "Inbound"
        | project NetworkMessageId, Subject, SenderFromAddress, SenderFromDomain,
                  RecipientEmailAddress, EmailTimestamp = Timestamp
      ) on NetworkMessageId
    | join kind=leftouter (
        EmailUrlInfo | project NetworkMessageId, Url, UrlDomain
      ) on NetworkMessageId, Url
    | project ClickTime = Timestamp, AccountUpn, IPAddress, Url, UrlDomain,
              Subject, SenderFromAddress, SenderFromDomain, RecipientEmailAddress,
              ActionType;
// Correlate to a non-browser child process spawned within 60 seconds on
// the recipient's device.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe",
                                         "outlook.exe","brave.exe","arc.exe")
| where FileName in~ ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","cmd.exe","mshta.exe",
                        "rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe",
                        "bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe","curl.exe","wget.exe")
| join kind=inner SuspectClicks on $left.AccountName == $right.AccountUpn
| where Timestamp between (ClickTime .. ClickTime + 60s)
| project ClickTime, ProcessTime = Timestamp,
          DelaySec = datetime_diff('second', Timestamp, ClickTime),
          DeviceName, AccountName, RecipientEmailAddress, SenderFromAddress,
          Subject, Url, UrlDomain, ActionType,
          FileName, ProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessFileName
| order by ClickTime desc
// UrlClickEvents has no clean Sentinel-native equivalent. The detection
// pivots to: Office Send→Receive proximity to SecurityEvent 4688 of a
// non-browser child process. Lower fidelity than the Defender version.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let SuspectMailUsers = OfficeActivity
    | where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where OfficeWorkload == "Exchange"
    | where Operation =~ "Receive"
    | summarize Subject = any(Subject), Sender = any(Sender)
                by MailboxOwnerUPN, MessageId, EmailTime = bin(TimeGenerated, 1m);
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
| where EventID == 4688
| where ParentProcessName has_any ("\chrome.exe","\msedge.exe",
                                     "\firefox.exe","\outlook.exe","\brave.exe")
| where NewProcessName has_any ("\powershell.exe","\pwsh.exe","\cmd.exe",
                                  "\mshta.exe","\rundll32.exe","\regsvr32.exe",
                                  "\wscript.exe","\cscript.exe","\bitsadmin.exe",
                                  "\certutil.exe","\curl.exe","\wget.exe")
| join kind=inner SuspectMailUsers on $left.Account == $right.MailboxOwnerUPN
| where TimeGenerated between (EmailTime .. EmailTime + 60s)
| project TimeGenerated, EmailTime, Computer, Account, ParentProcessName,
          NewProcessName, CommandLine, Sender, Subject
| order by TimeGenerated desc

Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
``` Phishing-link click that drives endpoint execution within 60s ```
| tstats `summariesonly` earliest(_time) AS click_time
    from datamodel=Web
    where Web.action="allowed"
    by Web.src, Web.user, Web.dest, Web.url
| `drop_dm_object_name(Web)`
| rename user AS recipient, dest AS clicked_domain, url AS clicked_url
| join type=inner recipient
    [| tstats `summariesonly` count
         from datamodel=Email.All_Email
         where All_Email.action="delivered" AND All_Email.url!="-"
         by All_Email.recipient, All_Email.src_user, All_Email.url, All_Email.subject
     | `drop_dm_object_name(All_Email)`
     | rex field=url "https?://(?<email_domain>[^/]+)"
     | rename recipient AS recipient]
| join type=inner src
    [| tstats `summariesonly` earliest(_time) AS exec_time
         values(Processes.process) AS exec_cmd, values(Processes.process_name) AS exec_proc
         from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
         where Processes.parent_process_name IN ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe",
                                                   "outlook.exe","brave.exe","arc.exe")
           AND Processes.process_name IN ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","cmd.exe","mshta.exe",
                                            "rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","wscript.exe",
                                            "cscript.exe","bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe",
                                            "curl.exe","wget.exe")
         by Processes.dest, Processes.user
     | `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)`
     | rename dest AS src]
| eval delta_sec = exec_time - click_time
| where delta_sec >= 0 AND delta_sec <= 60
| table click_time, exec_time, delta_sec, recipient, src, src_user, subject,
        clicked_domain, clicked_url, exec_proc, exec_cmd
| sort - click_time

Email attachment opened from external sender Delivery High
Attachment delivery + execution by recipient — most common malware initial access.
ATT&CKT1566.001 T1204.002
Data sourcesEmail.All_Email Endpoint.Processes EmailAttachmentInfo DeviceProcessEvents
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let MalAttachments = EmailAttachmentInfo
    | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where AccountName !endswith "$"
    | project NetworkMessageId, RecipientEmailAddress,
              AttachmentFileName = FileName, AttachmentSHA256 = SHA256;
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("OUTLOOK.EXE","winword.exe","excel.exe","powerpnt.exe")
| where FileName in~ ("cmd.exe","powershell.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe",
                      "mshta.exe","rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe")
| join kind=inner MalAttachments on $left.AccountUpn == $right.RecipientEmailAddress
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, FileName, ProcessCommandLine,
          InitiatingProcessFileName, AttachmentFileName, AttachmentSHA256
// Sentinel doesn't have an attachment-hash table. Best approximation:
// OfficeActivity Send/Receive activity + correlate to host process spawn.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let MailWithAttach = OfficeActivity
    | where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where OfficeWorkload == "Exchange"
    | where Operation in~ ("Send","Receive")
    | where isnotempty(MessageId)
    | project EmailTime = TimeGenerated, MailboxOwnerUPN, Sender,

Root process executing from anonymous memfd (CVE-2026-53264 core_pattern LPE payload) AIExploitation High
Hunts the culminating stage of the STAR Labs CVE-2026-53264 traffic-control UAF exploit: after the kernel ROP chain overwrites core_pattern to point at a memfd copy of the exploit, a deliberately-crashed child triggers the kernel to run that memfd-backed binary as the root core-dump handler. A root-owned process whose image resides in an anonymous memfd is almost never benign. Rationale: Anchors on the article's exact payload mechanism ('places a copy of itself in a memfd... run the memfd-backed binary as the root core-dump handler'); a root process imaged from a memfd is a near-unique high-fidelity signal for this LPE class. Cross-checked against: • https://securityonline.info/linux-kernel-cves/ • https://aquasecurity.github.io/tracee/v0.23/docs/events/builtin/signatures/core_pattern_modification/ • https://thecybersecguru.com/news/ghostlock-cve-2026-43499-linux-kernel-0day/
ATT&CKT1068 T1620
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Some sandbox/anti-cheat and packing tools (e.g. certain fileless loaders) legitimately exec from memfd, though rarely as root
  • Container runtimes that pass sealed memfds for runc/init helpers in edge configurations
  • Security research / red-team tooling run on the host during authorized testing
  • Custom in-memory deployment tooling that runs services from memfd to avoid disk writes
Suppression filter
| where not (InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("runc","containerd-shim","containerd-shim-runc-v2","crun") and InitiatingProcessAccountName =~ "root")
Response runbook
1) Triage: pull the full process tree and SHA256 of the memfd image; confirm the account is root and identify the parent/creating context (kernel core-dump handler = no normal parent). Check auditd for a preceding SIGSEGV/core dump and whether core_pattern currently references a pipe/memfd. 2) Contain: isolate the host, kill the root memfd process and any child shells, and snapshot memory before reboot to preserve the memfd image. 3) Hunt: on the same host look for prior unprivileged user+network namespace creation and tc clsact/flower activity; sweep the fleet for CVE-2026-53264 unpatched kernels and any other memfd-as-root executions.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(14d)
| where FolderPath has "memfd:" or FileName startswith "memfd:" or ProcessCommandLine has "memfd:"
| where AccountName =~ "root"
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, FileName, FolderPath, ProcessCommandLine, SHA256, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessAccountName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine
| order by Timestamp desc
ImProcessCreate
| where TimeGenerated > ago(14d)
| where TargetProcessName has "memfd" or TargetProcessCommandLine has "memfd:"
| where TargetUsername =~ "root"
| project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, TargetUsername, TargetProcessName, TargetProcessCommandLine, ActingProcessName, ActorUsername
| order by TimeGenerated desc

tc clsact qdisc + flower filter setup (CVE-2026-53264 UAF trigger path) AIExploitation Medium
Hunts creation of a clsact qdisc and a flower classifier via the tc utility — the exact traffic-control path (CONFIG_NET_CLS_FLOWER / clsact) the CVE-2026-53264 exploit walks to reach the RTM_NEWTFILTER/RTM_DELTFILTER use-after-free. Catches PoC/variant chains that shell out to iproute2's tc rather than crafting netlink directly. Rationale: Uses the article's named kernel-config/qdisc anchors (clsact + CONFIG_NET_CLS_FLOWER 'flower' filter) that define the vulnerable code path; distinguishes exploit setup from generic tc QoS/shaping by requiring the clsact+flower combination. Cross-checked against: • https://securityonline.info/linux-kernel-cves/ • https://windowsforum.com/security-alerts.84/cve-2026-64530-linux-kernel-fix-stops-red-tc-use-after-free.440572/
ATT&CKT1068 T1611
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • CNI plugins / service meshes (Cilium, Calico, Katran) that program clsact + flower/eBPF filters as normal operation
  • Network engineers configuring QoS or eBPF tc hooks during troubleshooting
  • Load-testing or DPI tooling that installs flower classifiers
  • Container startup scripts that attach clsact qdiscs for bandwidth policing
Suppression filter
| where InitiatingProcessFileName !in~ ("cilium-agent","calico-node","kubelet","containerd","dockerd","tc","bird","NetworkManager")
Response runbook
1) Triage: confirm the invoking account is unprivileged and the tc invocation is NOT from a known CNI/service-mesh binary or systemd unit; capture the full tc argument string and the parent process. 2) Contain: if the caller is an unexpected unprivileged user/shell, isolate the host and preserve process/auditd context. 3) Hunt: pivot on the same host/user for immediately following root-owned memfd execution (UC1), user+network namespace creation, and a crashed child (SIGSEGV) that would trigger the core_pattern handler.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(14d)
| where FileName =~ "tc"
| where ProcessCommandLine has "clsact" or (ProcessCommandLine has "flower" and ProcessCommandLine has "filter")
| where AccountName !endswith "$"
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, FileName, ProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessAccountName
| order by Timestamp desc
ImProcessCreate
| where TimeGenerated > ago(14d)
| where TargetProcessName has "tc"
| where TargetProcessCommandLine has "clsact" or (TargetProcessCommandLine has "flower" and TargetProcessCommandLine has "filter")
| project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, ActorUsername, TargetProcessName, TargetProcessCommandLine, ActingProcessName, ActingProcessCommandLine
| order by TimeGenerated desc

Unprivileged process spawns root child without sudo/su/pkexec (Linux LPE) AIExploitation Low
Hunts the definitional outcome of CVE-2026-53264: a process running as root (UID 0) whose creating process ran as a non-root user, where elevation did NOT pass through a legitimate setuid path (sudo/su/pkexec/doas). Broad net for the exploit's root shell and for other kernel LPE primitives that skip the normal auth chain. Rationale: Directly models the article's core claim ('turns an ordinary local user into root'); comparing child-runs-as-root vs parent-ran-as-nonroot while excluding legitimate setuid escalation binaries surfaces LPE that bypasses the auth chain. SPL/Datadog/Falcon left empty because those schemas cannot cleanly compare parent-vs-child UID in a single pass. Cross-checked against: • https://securityonline.info/linux-kernel-cves/ • https://thecybersecguru.com/news/ghostlock-cve-2026-43499-linux-kernel-0day/
ATT&CKT1068 T1548
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes
Expected false positives · estimated rate: high — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • setuid-root utilities not in the exclusion list (e.g. vendor backup agents, monitoring collectors) launched by users
  • cron/at jobs or service managers running tasks as root under an unusual account attribution
  • polkit/systemd-run helpers invoking privileged actions
  • Legitimate admin tooling and package managers that transiently elevate
  • Local dev/container tooling running rootful workloads from a user shell
Suppression filter
| where not (FolderPath startswith "/usr/lib/" and FileName endswith "-helper")
Response runbook
1) Triage: validate whether the root child came from a real setuid binary (check FolderPath/SHA256 and file mode) or from an unexpected image; review the initiating user's recent activity for exploit indicators. 2) Contain: if no legitimate elevation path explains it, isolate the host and suspend the offending user session. 3) Hunt: correlate on host+user for tc clsact/flower (UC2), a root memfd exec (UC1), and namespace creation; add confirmed-benign setuid binaries to the exclusion list to tune.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where AccountName =~ "root"
| where isnotempty(InitiatingProcessAccountName) and InitiatingProcessAccountName !~ "root" and InitiatingProcessAccountName !endswith "$"
| where InitiatingProcessFileName !in~ ("sudo","su","pkexec","doas","sshd","login","systemd","crond","cron","gdm","gdm-session-worker","lightdm","dbus-daemon","polkitd","runc","containerd-shim","containerd-shim-runc-v2","dockerd","containerd")
| where FileName !in~ ("sudo","su","passwd","chsh","chfn","newgrp","gpasswd","mount","umount","ping","ping6","pkexec","fusermount","fusermount3","crontab","at","ssh-agent","dbus-daemon-launch-helper","unix_chkpwd")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, ElevatedUser=AccountName, FileName, FolderPath, ProcessCommandLine, ParentUser=InitiatingProcessAccountName, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, SHA256
| order by Timestamp desc
ImProcessCreate
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where TargetUsername =~ "root"
| where isnotempty(ActorUsername) and ActorUsername !~ "root"
| where ActingProcessName !in~ ("sudo","su","pkexec","doas","sshd","login","systemd","crond","runc","containerd-shim","containerd-shim-runc-v2","dockerd","containerd","polkitd")
| where TargetProcessName !in~ ("sudo","su","passwd","chsh","chfn","newgrp","gpasswd","mount","umount","ping","pkexec","crontab","at")
| project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, TargetUsername, TargetProcessName, TargetProcessCommandLine, ActorUsername, ActingProcessName, ActingProcessCommandLine
| order by TimeGenerated desc
Exposure: hosts running kernel vulnerable to CVE-2026-53264 (unpatched TC UAF) AIReconnaissance High
Exposure hunt that enumerates managed Linux hosts still flagged vulnerable to CVE-2026-53264, so patching can be prioritised now that full exploit source is public. Pairs the article's fixed-release list (5.10.259, 5.15.210, 6.1.176, 6.6.143, 6.12.94, 6.18.36, 7.0.13) with TVM coverage. Rationale: Uses the article's exact CVE id and the enumerated fixed kernel releases; a deterministic TVM lookup gives the SOC an immediate patch-prioritisation list for a now-public exploit, filtering later for hosts that also enable unprivileged user namespaces + CONFIG_NET_CLS_FLOWER. Cross-checked against: • https://security.snyk.io/vuln/SNYK-RHEL6-KERNELDOC-17568795 • https://securityonline.info/linux-kernel-cves/
ATT&CKT1068
Data sources
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Hosts flagged vulnerable by version but with unprivileged user namespaces disabled (kernel.unprivileged_userns_clone=0) — not actually exploitable
  • Kernels lacking CONFIG_NET_ACT_GACT/CONFIG_NET_CLS_FLOWER — reduced/no exposure
  • Distro backport where the fix landed without a mainline version bump (version-string false positive)
  • Appliances/immutable images where the vendor has already mitigated out-of-band
Response runbook
1) Triage: rank flagged hosts by exposure — internet-facing, multi-user, or those permitting unprivileged user namespaces first. 2) Contain: for high-value hosts that cannot be patched immediately, set kernel.unprivileged_userns_clone=0 (or seccomp/AppArmor restrict) to remove the namespace prerequisite. 3) Hunt: schedule the fixed-version rollout (5.10.259 / 5.15.210 / 6.1.176 / 6.6.143 / 6.12.94 / 6.18.36 / 7.0.13 or distro backport) and monitor UC1–UC3 on any host that stays unpatched.

Phishing-link click correlated to endpoint execution Delivery High
User received an external email containing a URL, clicked it, and within 60 seconds the recipient's endpoint spawned a scripting interpreter or network downloader (PowerShell / cmd / mshta / curl / certutil / bitsadmin). This is the high-fidelity shape — a raw "user clicked an emailed URL" query is too noisy to alert on because every Microsoft 365 tenant generates thousands of legitimate clicks per day. The exec-correlation step suppresses the noise to roughly the rate at which a click actually drives onto-host execution, which is the actionable signal. Pair with UC_PHISH_LINK_BYPASS (Safe Links override) and UC_PHISH_LINK_NEWDOMAIN for orthogonal high-fidelity variants.
ATT&CKT1566.002 T1204.001 T1059.001
Data sourcesEmail.All_Email Web Endpoint.Processes EmailEvents EmailUrlInfo UrlClickEvents DeviceProcessEvents
// Phishing-link click that drives endpoint execution within 60s.
// Far higher fidelity than "every clicked URL" — most legitimate clicks
// never spawn a non-browser child process, so the join eliminates the
// 99% of noise that makes a raw click query unactionable.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let SuspectClicks = UrlClickEvents
    | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where AccountName !endswith "$"
    | where ActionType in ("ClickAllowed","ClickedThrough")
    | join kind=inner (
        EmailEvents
        | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
        | where DeliveryAction == "Delivered"
        | where EmailDirection == "Inbound"
        | project NetworkMessageId, Subject, SenderFromAddress, SenderFromDomain,
                  RecipientEmailAddress, EmailTimestamp = Timestamp
      ) on NetworkMessageId
    | join kind=leftouter (
        EmailUrlInfo | project NetworkMessageId, Url, UrlDomain
      ) on NetworkMessageId, Url
    | project ClickTime = Timestamp, AccountUpn, IPAddress, Url, UrlDomain,
              Subject, SenderFromAddress, SenderFromDomain, RecipientEmailAddress,
              ActionType;
// Correlate to a non-browser child process spawned within 60 seconds on
// the recipient's device.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe",
                                         "outlook.exe","brave.exe","arc.exe")
| where FileName in~ ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","cmd.exe","mshta.exe",
                        "rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe",
                        "bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe","curl.exe","wget.exe")
| join kind=inner SuspectClicks on $left.AccountName == $right.AccountUpn
| where Timestamp between (ClickTime .. ClickTime + 60s)
| project ClickTime, ProcessTime = Timestamp,
          DelaySec = datetime_diff('second', Timestamp, ClickTime),
          DeviceName, AccountName, RecipientEmailAddress, SenderFromAddress,
          Subject, Url, UrlDomain, ActionType,
          FileName, ProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessFileName
| order by ClickTime desc
// UrlClickEvents has no clean Sentinel-native equivalent. The detection
// pivots to: Office Send→Receive proximity to SecurityEvent 4688 of a
// non-browser child process. Lower fidelity than the Defender version.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let SuspectMailUsers = OfficeActivity
    | where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where OfficeWorkload == "Exchange"
    | where Operation =~ "Receive"
    | summarize Subject = any(Subject), Sender = any(Sender)
                by MailboxOwnerUPN, MessageId, EmailTime = bin(TimeGenerated, 1m);
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
| where EventID == 4688
| where ParentProcessName has_any ("\chrome.exe","\msedge.exe",
                                     "\firefox.exe","\outlook.exe","\brave.exe")
| where NewProcessName has_any ("\powershell.exe","\pwsh.exe","\cmd.exe",
                                  "\mshta.exe","\rundll32.exe","\regsvr32.exe",
                                  "\wscript.exe","\cscript.exe","\bitsadmin.exe",
                                  "\certutil.exe","\curl.exe","\wget.exe")
| join kind=inner SuspectMailUsers on $left.Account == $right.MailboxOwnerUPN
| where TimeGenerated between (EmailTime .. EmailTime + 60s)
| project TimeGenerated, EmailTime, Computer, Account, ParentProcessName,
          NewProcessName, CommandLine, Sender, Subject
| order by TimeGenerated desc

``` Phishing-link click that drives endpoint execution within 60s ```
| tstats `summariesonly` earliest(_time) AS click_time
    from datamodel=Web
    where Web.action="allowed"
    by Web.src, Web.user, Web.dest, Web.url
| `drop_dm_object_name(Web)`
| rename user AS recipient, dest AS clicked_domain, url AS clicked_url
| join type=inner recipient
    [| tstats `summariesonly` count
         from datamodel=Email.All_Email
         where All_Email.action="delivered" AND All_Email.url!="-"
         by All_Email.recipient, All_Email.src_user, All_Email.url, All_Email.subject
     | `drop_dm_object_name(All_Email)`
     | rex field=url "https?://(?<email_domain>[^/]+)"
     | rename recipient AS recipient]
| join type=inner src
    [| tstats `summariesonly` earliest(_time) AS exec_time
         values(Processes.process) AS exec_cmd, values(Processes.process_name) AS exec_proc
         from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
         where Processes.parent_process_name IN ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe",
                                                   "outlook.exe","brave.exe","arc.exe")
           AND Processes.process_name IN ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","cmd.exe","mshta.exe",
                                            "rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","wscript.exe",
                                            "cscript.exe","bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe",
                                            "curl.exe","wget.exe")
         by Processes.dest, Processes.user
     | `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)`
     | rename dest AS src]
| eval delta_sec = exec_time - click_time
| where delta_sec >= 0 AND delta_sec <= 60
| table click_time, exec_time, delta_sec, recipient, src, src_user, subject,
        clicked_domain, clicked_url, exec_proc, exec_cmd
| sort - click_time

Installation. Establishing persistence on the host — backdoor, service, scheduled task, registry key. → [LLM] NightLedger DLL search-order hijack: SspiCli.dll loaded by AppVShNotify.exe from non-system path · [LLM] BridgeHead tunneler DLL planted as unbcl.dll / libwinpthread-1.dll in atypical directories · File hash IOCs — endpoint file/process match
Command & Control. Beacon to attacker infrastructure for control and tasking. → [LLM] NightLedger C2 beacon to realhealthshop.com / tjconsultingservices.com · [LLM] BridgeHead/ArcBridge WebSocket tunnel to smartconnect.azurewebsites.net · Beaconing — periodic outbound to small set of destinations · Network connections to article IPs / domains
Actions on Objectives. Lateral movement, credential dumping, data theft, ransomware, sabotage. → [LLM] NightLedger staging: NetSetup.log copied out of C:\Windows\debug
NightLedger DLL search-order hijack: SspiCli.dll loaded by AppVShNotify.exe from non-system path AIInstallation Medium
Hunts Mirage Kitten's NightLedger backdoor, which masquerades as SspiCli.dll and is delay-loaded via RPCRT4.dll inside a co-located legitimate AppVShNotify.exe. Fires when SspiCli.dll (or the known NightLedger MD5) loads from any directory other than the Windows system folders. Rationale: Anchored on the article's explicit 'masquerades as SspiCli.dll ... targeting a legitimate AppVShNotify.exe' hijack plus the NightLedger MD5 c832ecd135781b11f59e3fffb3d2b6ac; SspiCli.dll legitimately only loads from the system directories, so any other path is high-fidelity.
ATT&CKT1574.001 T1574.002
Data sourcesEndpoint.Filesystem
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Microsoft App-V (AppVShNotify.exe) shipped inside a non-default install directory that co-locates a genuine SspiCli.dll copy
  • Software installers that temporarily stage a copy of SspiCli.dll under %TEMP% during setup
  • Developer/redistributable packages bundling system DLLs into an application folder
  • Backup/restore tooling copying WinSxS assemblies to a staging path
Suppression filter
| where InitiatingProcessFileName =~ "AppVShNotify.exe"
Response runbook
1) Triage: confirm the loading process is AppVShNotify.exe and inspect the SspiCli.dll SHA256/MD5 against the NightLedger IOC; verify the DLL is unsigned or forwards exports. 2) Contain: isolate the host, quarantine the rogue SspiCli.dll and its co-located AppVShNotify.exe, kill the process and check for mutex A8215357-F99A-44FE-BC65-D8F0434B0C03. 3) Hunt: pivot on the same host/user for outbound HTTPS to realhealthshop.com/tjconsultingservices.com and for BridgeHead tunneler DLLs (unbcl.dll, libwinpthread-1.dll).
DeviceImageLoadEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where FileName =~ "SspiCli.dll" or MD5 == "c832ecd135781b11f59e3fffb3d2b6ac"
| where not(FolderPath startswith @"C:\Windows\System32") and not(FolderPath startswith @"C:\Windows\SysWOW64") and not(FolderPath startswith @"C:\Windows\WinSxS")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessFolderPath, FileName, FolderPath, SHA256, MD5
| order by Timestamp desc
ImFileEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where TargetFileName =~ "SspiCli.dll" or TargetFileMD5 == "c832ecd135781b11f59e3fffb3d2b6ac"
| where not(TargetFilePath startswith @"C:\Windows\System32") and not(TargetFilePath startswith @"C:\Windows\SysWOW64") and not(TargetFilePath startswith @"C:\Windows\WinSxS")
| project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, ActingProcessName, TargetFilePath, TargetFileName, TargetFileSHA256, TargetFileMD5
| order by TimeGenerated desc

NightLedger C2 beacon to realhealthshop.com / tjconsultingservices.com AICommand & Control High
Hunts NightLedger command-and-control: periodic HTTPS to realhealthshop[.]com (primary) with tjconsultingservices[.]com fallback, using the distinctive GET /edfcvfgbhnjmkqwasderfgg beacon and POST /qasxcdfvgbhnmyuioplkhnj and /wsdefvvbnhyuijkplmbgfrtt result endpoints. Article-specific infrastructure, not a generic beacon shape. Rationale: Uses the article's two named C2 domains and the three verbatim URI endpoints (/edfcvfgbhnjmkqwasderfgg, /qasxcdfvgbhnmyuioplkhnj, /wsdefvvbnhyuijkplmbgfrtt) — hard-coded operator infrastructure with no benign overlap.
ATT&CKT1071.001 T1041
Data sourcesWeb.Web Network_Resolution.DNS
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Security-team detonation/sandbox traffic replaying the same IOCs during analysis
  • Threat-intel crawler or IOC-validation tooling resolving the domains
  • Sinkhole redirection if the domains have been seized
  • Proxy pre-fetch/URL-reputation scanners touching the domains
Suppression filter
| where InitiatingProcessFileName !in~ ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe")
Response runbook
1) Triage: identify the initiating process (expect AppVShNotify.exe / rogue SspiCli.dll) and confirm periodicity of the GET beacon vs POST result uploads. 2) Contain: block realhealthshop.com and tjconsultingservices.com at proxy/DNS, isolate the beaconing host. 3) Hunt: sweep all hosts for the same domains, for the smartconnect.azurewebsites.net WebSocket tunnel, and for staged copies of NetSetup.log.
DeviceNetworkEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where RemoteUrl has_any ("realhealthshop.com","tjconsultingservices.com")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessFolderPath, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, RemoteUrl, RemoteIP, RemotePort
| order by Timestamp desc
union isfuzzy=true
(CommonSecurityLog
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where DestinationHostName has_any ("realhealthshop.com","tjconsultingservices.com") or RequestURL has_any ("/edfcvfgbhnjmkqwasderfgg","/qasxcdfvgbhnmyuioplkhnj","/wsdefvvbnhyuijkplmbgfrtt")
| project TimeGenerated, SourceIP, DestinationHostName, RequestURL, RequestMethod, RequestClientApplication, DeviceProduct),
(ImDnsActivity
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where DnsQuery has_any ("realhealthshop.com","tjconsultingservices.com")
| project TimeGenerated, SrcIpAddr, DnsQuery, EventProduct)
| order by TimeGenerated desc
title: NightLedger C2 Domains and Beacon URIs

BridgeHead/ArcBridge WebSocket tunnel to smartconnect.azurewebsites.net AICommand & Control High
Hunts Mirage Kitten's BridgeHead/ArcBridge WebSocket tunnelers establishing a SOCKS5 relay via GET /connect over HTTPS to smartconnect[.]azurewebsites[.]net, including the hard-coded stale Edge/86.0.622.38 User-Agent. Detects covert operator tunneling that traverses enterprise proxies with SSO auth. Rationale: Anchored on the verbatim BridgeHead handshake target smartconnect.azurewebsites.net/connect and the hard-coded stale Edg/86.0.622.38 User-Agent from the article's HTTP request block — both are attacker-fixed values.
ATT&CKT1572 T1071.001 T1090
Data sourcesWeb.Web Network_Resolution.DNS
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • A benign internal app legitimately hosted on the same Azure App Service name (unlikely — attacker-registered)
  • Security research replaying the WebSocket handshake in a lab
  • Proxy URL-reputation scanner fetching the /connect path
  • Old-browser fleet genuinely emitting Edg/86.0.622.38 (rare on a patched estate)
Suppression filter
| where InitiatingProcessFileName !in~ ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe","brave.exe")
Response runbook
1) Triage: identify the process opening the socket (expect unbcl.dll/libwinpthread-1.dll host process, not a browser) and confirm the WebSocket upgrade (HTTP 101) and Edge/86 UA. 2) Contain: block smartconnect.azurewebsites.net, isolate the relay host, capture the loaded tunneler DLL. 3) Hunt: enumerate inbound TCP the relay forwarded (SOCKS5 targets), and look for the paired NightLedger SspiCli.dll hijack on the same or adjacent hosts.
DeviceNetworkEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where RemoteUrl has "smartconnect.azurewebsites.net"
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessFolderPath, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, RemoteUrl, RemoteIP, RemotePort
| order by Timestamp desc
union isfuzzy=true
(CommonSecurityLog
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where DestinationHostName has "smartconnect.azurewebsites.net" or RequestURL has "smartconnect.azurewebsites.net/connect" or RequestClientApplication has "Edg/86.0.622.38"
| project TimeGenerated, SourceIP, DestinationHostName, RequestURL, RequestClientApplication, RequestMethod),
(ImWebSession
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where HttpHostName has "smartconnect.azurewebsites.net" or Url has "smartconnect.azurewebsites.net/connect" or HttpRequestHeaderUserAgent has "Edg/86.0.622.38"
| project TimeGenerated, SrcIpAddr, HttpHostName, Url, HttpRequestHeaderUserAgent)
| order by TimeGenerated desc

BridgeHead tunneler DLL planted as unbcl.dll / libwinpthread-1.dll in atypical directories AIInstallation High
Hunts the on-disk footprint of Mirage Kitten's BridgeHead tunneler: unbcl.dll dropped under %LocalAppData%\Microsoft\VisualStudio, or libwinpthread-1.dll dropped under C:\Program Files (x86)\univpn\promote. Both are the exact planted paths reported from the Egypt and Pakistan victim environments. Rationale: Uses the two verbatim planted tunneler paths from the article (%LocalAppData%\Microsoft\VisualStudio\unbcl.dll and C:\program files (x86)\univpn\promote\libwinpthread-1.dll) — legitimate copies of these DLLs do not live in these directories.
ATT&CKT1574.002 T1105
Data sourcesEndpoint.Filesystem
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • A genuine univpn VPN client install placing libwinpthread-1.dll under its own directory (verify signature/hash)
  • Visual Studio component that legitimately ships unbcl.dll (native VS uses SysWOW64, not a user VisualStudio folder)
  • MinGW/GCC toolchain redistributing libwinpthread-1.dll into a dev workspace
  • Backup/AV quarantine relocating the DLL and re-emitting a file-write event
Response runbook
1) Triage: hash the dropped DLL, confirm it is unsigned/masquerading and check for the GetUserNameA substring anti-analysis guard; identify the writing process. 2) Contain: quarantine the DLL, isolate the host, kill the loading process. 3) Hunt: pivot to smartconnect.azurewebsites.net WebSocket traffic from the host and to NightLedger SspiCli.dll hijack activity elsewhere in the estate.
DeviceFileEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where (FileName =~ "unbcl.dll" and FolderPath has @"\Microsoft\VisualStudio")
     or (FileName =~ "libwinpthread-1.dll" and FolderPath has @"univpn\promote")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessFolderPath, FileName, FolderPath, SHA256, MD5
| order by Timestamp desc
ImFileEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where (TargetFileName =~ "unbcl.dll" and TargetFilePath has @"\Microsoft\VisualStudio")
     or (TargetFileName =~ "libwinpthread-1.dll" and TargetFilePath has @"univpn\promote")
| project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, ActingProcessName, TargetFilePath, TargetFileName, TargetFileSHA256
| order by TimeGenerated desc

NightLedger staging: NetSetup.log copied out of C:\Windows\debug AIActions on Objectives Medium
Hunts NightLedger command 93 (collect C:\Windows\debug\NetSetup.log with process list) and command 27 (copy a file): a file named NetSetup.log appearing outside its native C:\Windows\debug directory, indicating the domain-join diagnostic log is being staged for exfiltration. Rationale: Anchored on the article's NightLedger command 93 specifically collecting C:\Windows\debug\NetSetup.log; that diagnostic file only natively exists under C:\Windows\debug, so a copy elsewhere is a strong staging signal.
ATT&CKT1005 T1074.001 T1482
Data sourcesEndpoint.Filesystem
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • A sysadmin or Microsoft support engineer manually copying NetSetup.log to a share to troubleshoot a domain-join failure
  • Endpoint diagnostic/log-collection tooling (MDM, SCCM) bundling NetSetup.log into a support package
  • Backup software snapshotting C:\Windows\debug into a staging directory
  • Security IR tooling pulling the log during unrelated forensics
Suppression filter
| where InitiatingProcessFileName !in~ ("cmtrace.exe","ccmexec.exe","mdmdiagnosticstool.exe")
Response runbook
1) Triage: identify the process that wrote the copy and the destination path; correlate with process-list collection and any tasklist/net commands around the same time. 2) Contain: if the writer is the hijacked AppVShNotify.exe / rogue SspiCli.dll, isolate the host and preserve the staged file. 3) Hunt: check for subsequent POST uploads to /qasxcdfvgbhnmyuioplkhnj on realhealthshop.com and enumerate what else was staged in the same directory.
DeviceFileEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where FileName =~ "NetSetup.log"
| where not(FolderPath startswith @"C:\Windows\debug")
| where InitiatingProcessAccountName !endswith "$"
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, InitiatingProcessAccountName, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessFolderPath, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, FileName, FolderPath, PreviousFolderPath
| order by Timestamp desc
ImFileEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where TargetFileName =~ "NetSetup.log"
| where not(TargetFilePath startswith @"C:\Windows\debug")
| project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, ActorUsername, ActingProcessName, ActingProcessCommandLine, TargetFilePath, TargetFileName
| order by TimeGenerated desc

Beaconing — periodic outbound to small set of destinations Command & Control Medium
C2 channel detection via inter-beacon-time stddev / fan-out to single dest.
ATT&CKT1071.001 T1071.004
Data sourcesNetwork_Traffic.All_Traffic DeviceNetworkEvents
DeviceNetworkEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(1d)
| where RemoteIPType == "Public" and ActionType == "ConnectionSuccess"
| project DeviceName, RemoteIP, RemotePort, Timestamp
| sort by DeviceName asc, RemoteIP asc, RemotePort asc, Timestamp asc
| extend prev_dev = prev(DeviceName, 1), prev_ip = prev(RemoteIP, 1),
         prev_port = prev(RemotePort, 1), prev_ts = prev(Timestamp, 1)
| where DeviceName == prev_dev and RemoteIP == prev_ip and RemotePort == prev_port
| extend delta_sec = datetime_diff('second', Timestamp, prev_ts)
| summarize conn_count = count(), avg_delta = avg(delta_sec), stdev_delta = stdev(delta_sec)
    by DeviceName, RemoteIP, RemotePort
| where conn_count > 30 and avg_delta between (30.0 .. 600.0) and stdev_delta < 5.0
| order by conn_count desc
ImNetworkSession
| where TimeGenerated > ago(2h)
| where DvcAction != "Block"
| where ipv4_is_private(DstIpAddr) == false
| summarize ConnCount = count(),
            DistinctMinutes = dcount(bin(TimeGenerated, 1m))
            by DvcHostname, DstIpAddr, DstPortNumber
| where ConnCount > 50 and DistinctMinutes > 30   // sustained, not bursty
| order by ConnCount desc
NETWORK
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
| tstats `summariesonly` count, values(All_Traffic.dest_port) AS ports
    from datamodel=Network_Traffic.All_Traffic
    where All_Traffic.action="allowed" AND All_Traffic.dest_category!="internal"
    by _time span=10s, All_Traffic.src, All_Traffic.dest
| `drop_dm_object_name(All_Traffic)`
| streamstats current=f last(_time) AS prev_time by src, dest
| eval delta = _time - prev_time
| stats avg(delta) AS avg_delta stdev(delta) AS sd_delta count by src, dest
| where count > 30 AND sd_delta < 5 AND avg_delta>=30 AND avg_delta<=600
| sort - count
| tstats summariesonly=false count, values(All_Traffic.dest_port) AS ports
    from datamodel=Network_Traffic.All_Traffic
    where All_Traffic.action="allowed" AND All_Traffic.dest_category!="internal"
    by _time span=10s, All_Traffic.src, All_Traffic.dest
| `drop_dm_object_name(All_Traffic)`
| streamstats current=f last(_time) AS prev_time by src, dest
| eval delta = _time - prev_time
| stats avg(delta) AS avg_delta stdev(delta) AS sd_delta count by src, dest
| where count > 30 AND sd_delta < 5 AND avg_delta>=30 AND avg_delta<=600
| sort - count

Phishing-link click correlated to endpoint execution Delivery High
User received an external email containing a URL, clicked it, and within 60 seconds the recipient's endpoint spawned a scripting interpreter or network downloader (PowerShell / cmd / mshta / curl / certutil / bitsadmin). This is the high-fidelity shape — a raw "user clicked an emailed URL" query is too noisy to alert on because every Microsoft 365 tenant generates thousands of legitimate clicks per day. The exec-correlation step suppresses the noise to roughly the rate at which a click actually drives onto-host execution, which is the actionable signal. Pair with UC_PHISH_LINK_BYPASS (Safe Links override) and UC_PHISH_LINK_NEWDOMAIN for orthogonal high-fidelity variants.
ATT&CKT1566.002 T1204.001 T1059.001
Data sourcesEmail.All_Email Web Endpoint.Processes EmailEvents EmailUrlInfo UrlClickEvents DeviceProcessEvents
// Phishing-link click that drives endpoint execution within 60s.
// Far higher fidelity than "every clicked URL" — most legitimate clicks
// never spawn a non-browser child process, so the join eliminates the
// 99% of noise that makes a raw click query unactionable.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let SuspectClicks = UrlClickEvents
    | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where AccountName !endswith "$"
    | where ActionType in ("ClickAllowed","ClickedThrough")
    | join kind=inner (
        EmailEvents
        | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
        | where DeliveryAction == "Delivered"
        | where EmailDirection == "Inbound"
        | project NetworkMessageId, Subject, SenderFromAddress, SenderFromDomain,
                  RecipientEmailAddress, EmailTimestamp = Timestamp
      ) on NetworkMessageId
    | join kind=leftouter (
        EmailUrlInfo | project NetworkMessageId, Url, UrlDomain
      ) on NetworkMessageId, Url
    | project ClickTime = Timestamp, AccountUpn, IPAddress, Url, UrlDomain,
              Subject, SenderFromAddress, SenderFromDomain, RecipientEmailAddress,
              ActionType;
// Correlate to a non-browser child process spawned within 60 seconds on
// the recipient's device.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe",
                                         "outlook.exe","brave.exe","arc.exe")
| where FileName in~ ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","cmd.exe","mshta.exe",
                        "rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe",
                        "bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe","curl.exe","wget.exe")
| join kind=inner SuspectClicks on $left.AccountName == $right.AccountUpn
| where Timestamp between (ClickTime .. ClickTime + 60s)
| project ClickTime, ProcessTime = Timestamp,
          DelaySec = datetime_diff('second', Timestamp, ClickTime),
          DeviceName, AccountName, RecipientEmailAddress, SenderFromAddress,
          Subject, Url, UrlDomain, ActionType,
          FileName, ProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessFileName
| order by ClickTime desc
// UrlClickEvents has no clean Sentinel-native equivalent. The detection
// pivots to: Office Send→Receive proximity to SecurityEvent 4688 of a
// non-browser child process. Lower fidelity than the Defender version.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let SuspectMailUsers = OfficeActivity
    | where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where OfficeWorkload == "Exchange"
    | where Operation =~ "Receive"
    | summarize Subject = any(Subject), Sender = any(Sender)
                by MailboxOwnerUPN, MessageId, EmailTime = bin(TimeGenerated, 1m);
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
| where EventID == 4688
| where ParentProcessName has_any ("\chrome.exe","\msedge.exe",
                                     "\firefox.exe","\outlook.exe","\brave.exe")
| where NewProcessName has_any ("\powershell.exe","\pwsh.exe","\cmd.exe",
                                  "\mshta.exe","\rundll32.exe","\regsvr32.exe",
                                  "\wscript.exe","\cscript.exe","\bitsadmin.exe",
                                  "\certutil.exe","\curl.exe","\wget.exe")
| join kind=inner SuspectMailUsers on $left.Account == $right.MailboxOwnerUPN
| where TimeGenerated between (EmailTime .. EmailTime + 60s)
| project TimeGenerated, EmailTime, Computer, Account, ParentProcessName,
          NewProcessName, CommandLine, Sender, Subject
| order by TimeGenerated desc
WEB
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
``` Phishing-link click that drives endpoint execution within 60s ```
| tstats `summariesonly` earliest(_time) AS click_time
    from datamodel=Web
    where Web.action="allowed"
    by Web.src, Web.user, Web.dest, Web.url
| `drop_dm_object_name(Web)`
| rename user AS recipient, dest AS clicked_domain, url AS clicked_url
| join type=inner recipient
    [| tstats `summariesonly` count
         from datamodel=Email.All_Email
         where All_Email.action="delivered" AND All_Email.url!="-"
         by All_Email.recipient, All_Email.src_user, All_Email.url, All_Email.subject
     | `drop_dm_object_name(All_Email)`
     | rex field=url "https?://(?<email_domain>[^/]+)"
     | rename recipient AS recipient]
| join type=inner src
    [| tstats `summariesonly` earliest(_time) AS exec_time
         values(Processes.process) AS exec_cmd, values(Processes.process_name) AS exec_proc
         from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
         where Processes.parent_process_name IN ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe",
                                                   "outlook.exe","brave.exe","arc.exe")
           AND Processes.process_name IN ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","cmd.exe","mshta.exe",
                                            "rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","wscript.exe",
                                            "cscript.exe","bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe",
                                            "curl.exe","wget.exe")
         by Processes.dest, Processes.user
     | `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)`
     | rename dest AS src]
| eval delta_sec = exec_time - click_time
| where delta_sec >= 0 AND delta_sec <= 60
| table click_time, exec_time, delta_sec, recipient, src, src_user, subject,
        clicked_domain, clicked_url, exec_proc, exec_cmd
| sort - click_time

Email attachment opened from external sender Delivery High
Attachment delivery + execution by recipient — most common malware initial access.
ATT&CKT1566.001 T1204.002
Data sourcesEmail.All_Email Endpoint.Processes EmailAttachmentInfo DeviceProcessEvents
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let MalAttachments = EmailAttachmentInfo
    | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where AccountName !endswith "$"
    | project NetworkMessageId, RecipientEmailAddress,
              AttachmentFileName = FileName, AttachmentSHA256 = SHA256;
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("OUTLOOK.EXE","winword.exe","excel.exe","powerpnt.exe")
| where FileName in~ ("cmd.exe","powershell.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe",
                      "mshta.exe","rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe")
| join kind=inner MalAttachments on $left.AccountUpn == $right.RecipientEmailAddress
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, FileName, ProcessCommandLine,
          InitiatingProcessFileName, AttachmentFileName, AttachmentSHA256
// Sentinel doesn't have an attachment-hash table. Best approximation:
// OfficeActivity Send/Receive activity + correlate to host process spawn.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let MailWithAttach = OfficeActivity
    | where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where OfficeWorkload == "Exchange"
    | where Operation in~ ("Send","Receive")
    | where isnotempty(MessageId)
    | project EmailTime = TimeGenerated, MailboxOwnerUPN, Sender,
              Recipients, Subject, MessageId;
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
| where EventID == 4688
| where ParentProcessName endswith "OUTLOOK.EXE"
| where NewProcessName endswith "\cmd.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\powershell.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\wscript.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\cscript.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\mshta.exe"
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, Account, NewProcessName, CommandLine,
          ParentProcessName
| order by TimeGenerated desc

File hash IOCs — endpoint file/process match Installation High
Match SHA256/SHA1/MD5 named in the article against EDR file/process telemetry.
ATT&CKT1027
Data sourcesEndpoint.Filesystem Endpoint.Processes DeviceFileEvents DeviceProcessEvents
// Pre-filter each table BEFORE the union — the engine cannot push
// predicates across `union`, and DeviceFileEvents lacks ProcessCommandLine
// (Initiating only) so column-projection has to differ per side.
union
    ( DeviceFileEvents
        | where Timestamp > ago(7d)
        | where InitiatingProcessAccountName !endswith "$"
        | where SHA256 in~ ("c832ecd135781b11f59e3fffb3d2b6ac") or SHA1 in~ ("c832ecd135781b11f59e3fffb3d2b6ac") or MD5 in~ ("c832ecd135781b11f59e3fffb3d2b6ac")
        | project Timestamp, DeviceName, ActionType, FileName, FolderPath, SHA256,
                  Cmd = InitiatingProcessCommandLine, Source = "DeviceFileEvents" ),
    ( DeviceProcessEvents
        | where Timestamp > ago(7d)
        | where AccountName !endswith "$"
        | where SHA256 in~ ("c832ecd135781b11f59e3fffb3d2b6ac") or SHA1 in~ ("c832ecd135781b11f59e3fffb3d2b6ac") or MD5 in~ ("c832ecd135781b11f59e3fffb3d2b6ac")
        | project Timestamp, DeviceName, ActionType, FileName, FolderPath, SHA256,
                  Cmd = ProcessCommandLine, Source = "DeviceProcessEvents" )
| order by Timestamp desc

// Pre-filter both ASIM tables before the union — same pattern as the
// Defender version so the engine can push hash predicates per-side.
let BadHashes = dynamic(["c832ecd135781b11f59e3fffb3d2b6ac"]);
union
    ( ImFileEvent
        | where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
        | where ActorUsername !endswith "$"
        | where TargetFileSHA256 in~ (BadHashes)
           or TargetFileSHA1 in~ (BadHashes)
           or TargetFileMD5 in~ (BadHashes)
        | project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, EventType,
                  TargetFileName, TargetFilePath, TargetFileSHA256,
                  Cmd = ActingProcessName, Source = "ImFileEvent" ),
    ( ImProcessCreate
        | where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
        | where ActorUsername !endswith "$"
        | where SHA256 in~ (BadHashes) or SHA1 in~ (BadHashes) or MD5 in~ (BadHashes)
        | project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, EventType = TargetProcessName,
                  TargetFileName = TargetProcessName, TargetFilePath = TargetProcessName,
                  TargetFileSHA256 = SHA256,
                  Cmd = TargetProcessCommandLine, Source = "ImProcessCreate" )
| order by TimeGenerated desc

Attackers Exploit Arista VeloCloud Orchestrator Command Injection Flaw

The Hacker News
2026-07-28 8 use cases 3 techniques 5 kill-chain phases detected

A maximum-severity security flaw impacting on-premises versions of Arista VeloCloud Orchestrator (VCO) has come under active exploitation in the wild. The vulnerability, tracked as CVE-2026-16812 (CVSS score: 10.0), is a case of operating system command injection that could pave the way for arbitrary code execution. Detected
Reconnaissance. Attacker researches the target — OSINT, scanning, enumeration. → Asset exposure — vulnerability matches article CVE(s)
Weaponization. Coupling exploit code with deliverable payload (e.g. weaponized PDF/Office doc, trojanized installer).
Delivery. Transmitting the weapon (phishing email, USB, watering hole, drive-by, malicious ad). → [LLM] Inbound web access to VeloCloud Orchestrator from CVE-2026-16812 attacker source IPs · Phishing-link click correlated to endpoint execution · Email attachment opened from external sender
Exploitation. Triggering the exploit — vulnerability/macro/trust abuse to execute code. → Office app spawning script/LOLBin child process · Fake CAPTCHA / clipboard-injected PowerShell (ClickFix / FakeCaptcha)
Installation. Establishing persistence on the host — backdoor, service, scheduled task, registry key.
Command & Control. Beacon to attacker infrastructure for control and tasking. → [LLM] Network communication with CVE-2026-16812 VeloCloud Orchestrator attacker infrastructure · Network connections to article IPs / domains
Actions on Objectives. Lateral movement, credential dumping, data theft, ransomware, sabotage.
Network communication with CVE-2026-16812 VeloCloud Orchestrator attacker infrastructure AICommand & Control Medium
Hunts any traffic to/from the three IP addresses Arista named as conducting active exploitation of the VCO on-prem OS command-injection flaw (CVE-2026-16812). Covers both inbound exploitation and post-exploit outbound C2/exfil from the orchestrator host, which the vendor advisory explicitly told operators to check for. Rationale: Uses the three exact attacker IPs (8.19.75.217, 206.72.242.124, 206.72.242.162) Arista published as responsible for the attacks — pure IOC match, near-zero FP. Corroborated against Arista Security Advisory 0144, the CISA KEV addition, BleepingComputer and The Register write-ups of the same campaign. Cross-checked against: • https://www.arista.com/en/support/advisories-notices/security-advisory/24364-security-advisory-0144 • https://www.cisa.gov/news-events/alerts/2026/07/27/cisa-adds-two-known-exploited-vulnerabilities-catalog • https://www.bleepingcomputer.com/news/security/arista-patches-velocloud-orchestrator-zero-day-exploited-in-attacks/ • https://www.theregister.com/security/2026/07/28/arista-patches-actively-exploited-velocloud-bug-as-cisa-puts-admins-on-the-clock/5279414
ATT&CKT1190 T1071.001 T1041
Data sourcesNetwork_Traffic.All_Traffic
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Internal threat-intel scanner or IOC-validation tooling deliberately probing the published IPs
  • Security researcher / red team sourcing from a cloud VPS that later gets reassigned one of these IPs
  • Passive DNS or CTI enrichment appliance resolving/connecting to flagged infra
  • Netflow spillover where the appliance sensor mislabels src/dest on a NAT boundary
  • Firewall already blocking the IP but still logging the denied attempt (expected, not a compromise)
Suppression filter
| where not (InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("threatintel-scanner.exe","nessus.exe") or DeviceName has_any ("scanner","cti-"))
Response runbook
1) Triage: identify the internal asset that talked to the IP — if it is the VCO on-prem host or an adjacent management box, treat as high priority. Determine direction: inbound = exploitation attempt, outbound = likely post-exploit C2/exfil. 2) Contain: block all three IPs at the perimeter, isolate the VCO host, and preserve VCO web access logs, backend application logs, system/database logs and file-system timestamps before remediation (per Arista guidance). 3) Hunt: confirm VCO patch level (>= 5.2.3.14 / 6.1.3.4 / 6.4.2.4 / 7.0.0.1); rotate VCO and managed VeloCloud Edge credentials, review recent administrator activity for unexpected changes, and validate managed-device state for lateral compromise.

Inbound web access to VeloCloud Orchestrator from CVE-2026-16812 attacker source IPs AIDelivery Medium
Surfaces HTTP/web-interface access to the VCO from the three attacker source IPs Arista tied to active exploitation — the application-layer evidence of the unauthenticated OS command-injection attempt (CVE-2026-16812). Targets the VCO web access logs the vendor told operators to preserve, a distinct pivot from raw netflow. Rationale: Anchors on the three published attacker source IPs against web/access-log telemetry (cIP / SourceIP / SyslogMessage) — the exact records Arista said to preserve as VCO web access logs. Application-layer evidence of the exploitation attempt, distinct from the netflow UC. Corroborated by Arista Advisory 0144 and CISA KEV. Cross-checked against: • https://www.arista.com/en/support/advisories-notices/security-advisory/24364-security-advisory-0144 • https://www.cisa.gov/news-events/alerts/2026/07/27/cisa-adds-two-known-exploited-vulnerabilities-catalog • https://www.bleepingcomputer.com/news/security/arista-patches-velocloud-orchestrator-zero-day-exploited-in-attacks/
ATT&CKT1190 T1059
Data sourcesWeb.Web
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Internal vulnerability scanner (Nessus/Qualys) whose egress IP coincidentally lands in the same range
  • Security team replaying the IOC against the appliance to test blocking
  • Load balancer / reverse proxy that rewrites SourceIP causing a benign internal host to appear as the flagged IP
  • CTI appliance fetching the VCO login banner for asset inventory
  • A now-blocked IP whose denied HTTP attempts are still logged by the WAF (expected control working)
Response runbook
1) Triage: pull the full web-access log lines for the matching IP — capture method, URI, query string, response code and user-agent to characterise the request against the VCO management interface; confirm the target really is the VCO host. 2) Contain: block the source IPs, restrict the VCO web interface to trusted admin networks only, and snapshot the appliance (preserve web/app/system/db logs and file timestamps before remediation). 3) Hunt: verify VCO is patched to a fixed release; review administrator activity and any config/credential changes since the first hit; pivot to UC1 to check for outbound C2/exfil from the same host and validate managed VeloCloud Edge device state.

Phishing-link click correlated to endpoint execution Delivery High
User received an external email containing a URL, clicked it, and within 60 seconds the recipient's endpoint spawned a scripting interpreter or network downloader (PowerShell / cmd / mshta / curl / certutil / bitsadmin). This is the high-fidelity shape — a raw "user clicked an emailed URL" query is too noisy to alert on because every Microsoft 365 tenant generates thousands of legitimate clicks per day. The exec-correlation step suppresses the noise to roughly the rate at which a click actually drives onto-host execution, which is the actionable signal. Pair with UC_PHISH_LINK_BYPASS (Safe Links override) and UC_PHISH_LINK_NEWDOMAIN for orthogonal high-fidelity variants.
ATT&CKT1566.002 T1204.001 T1059.001
Data sourcesEmail.All_Email Web Endpoint.Processes EmailEvents EmailUrlInfo UrlClickEvents DeviceProcessEvents
// Phishing-link click that drives endpoint execution within 60s.
// Far higher fidelity than "every clicked URL" — most legitimate clicks
// never spawn a non-browser child process, so the join eliminates the
// 99% of noise that makes a raw click query unactionable.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let SuspectClicks = UrlClickEvents
    | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where AccountName !endswith "$"
    | where ActionType in ("ClickAllowed","ClickedThrough")
    | join kind=inner (
        EmailEvents
        | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
        | where DeliveryAction == "Delivered"
        | where EmailDirection == "Inbound"
        | project NetworkMessageId, Subject, SenderFromAddress, SenderFromDomain,
                  RecipientEmailAddress, EmailTimestamp = Timestamp
      ) on NetworkMessageId
    | join kind=leftouter (
        EmailUrlInfo | project NetworkMessageId, Url, UrlDomain
      ) on NetworkMessageId, Url
    | project ClickTime = Timestamp, AccountUpn, IPAddress, Url, UrlDomain,
              Subject, SenderFromAddress, SenderFromDomain, RecipientEmailAddress,
              ActionType;
// Correlate to a non-browser child process spawned within 60 seconds on
// the recipient's device.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe",
                                         "outlook.exe","brave.exe","arc.exe")
| where FileName in~ ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","cmd.exe","mshta.exe",
                        "rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe",
                        "bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe","curl.exe","wget.exe")
| join kind=inner SuspectClicks on $left.AccountName == $right.AccountUpn
| where Timestamp between (ClickTime .. ClickTime + 60s)
| project ClickTime, ProcessTime = Timestamp,
          DelaySec = datetime_diff('second', Timestamp, ClickTime),
          DeviceName, AccountName, RecipientEmailAddress, SenderFromAddress,
          Subject, Url, UrlDomain, ActionType,
          FileName, ProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessFileName
| order by ClickTime desc
// UrlClickEvents has no clean Sentinel-native equivalent. The detection
// pivots to: Office Send→Receive proximity to SecurityEvent 4688 of a
// non-browser child process. Lower fidelity than the Defender version.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let SuspectMailUsers = OfficeActivity
    | where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where OfficeWorkload == "Exchange"
    | where Operation =~ "Receive"
    | summarize Subject = any(Subject), Sender = any(Sender)
                by MailboxOwnerUPN, MessageId, EmailTime = bin(TimeGenerated, 1m);
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
| where EventID == 4688
| where ParentProcessName has_any ("\chrome.exe","\msedge.exe",
                                     "\firefox.exe","\outlook.exe","\brave.exe")
| where NewProcessName has_any ("\powershell.exe","\pwsh.exe","\cmd.exe",
                                  "\mshta.exe","\rundll32.exe","\regsvr32.exe",
                                  "\wscript.exe","\cscript.exe","\bitsadmin.exe",
                                  "\certutil.exe","\curl.exe","\wget.exe")
| join kind=inner SuspectMailUsers on $left.Account == $right.MailboxOwnerUPN
| where TimeGenerated between (EmailTime .. EmailTime + 60s)
| project TimeGenerated, EmailTime, Computer, Account, ParentProcessName,
          NewProcessName, CommandLine, Sender, Subject
| order by TimeGenerated desc

Likely
Reconnaissance. Attacker researches the target — OSINT, scanning, enumeration. → Asset exposure — vulnerability matches article CVE(s)
Weaponization. Coupling exploit code with deliverable payload (e.g. weaponized PDF/Office doc, trojanized installer).
Delivery. Transmitting the weapon (phishing email, USB, watering hole, drive-by, malicious ad). → [LLM] Inbound FastJson @type payload with jar:/ldap:/rmi: reference to Spring Boot app (CVE-2026-16723)
Exploitation. Triggering the exploit — vulnerability/macro/trust abuse to execute code. → [LLM] Spring Boot Java fat-JAR spawning shell/recon child process (FastJson CVE-2026-16723 RCE) · Article-specific behavioural hunt — Hackers target US firms in FastJson RCE zero-day attacks
Installation. Establishing persistence on the host — backdoor, service, scheduled task, registry key.
Command & Control. Beacon to attacker infrastructure for control and tasking. → [LLM] Java application making outbound LDAP/RMI connection (FastJson CVE-2026-16723 remote class load)
Actions on Objectives. Lateral movement, credential dumping, data theft, ransomware, sabotage.
Inbound FastJson @type payload with jar:/ldap:/rmi: reference to Spring Boot app (CVE-2026-16723) AIDelivery Medium
Hunts inbound HTTP request bodies/URIs carrying a FastJson '@type' key alongside a nested jar:, ldap:, rmi: URL or JdbcRowSetImpl/dataSourceName reference — the exploitation shape for CVE-2026-16723 against internet-facing Spring Boot fat-JAR apps. Article-specific because it keys on the @type + remote-resource-lookup combination, not generic deserialization. Rationale: Keys on the CVE-2026-16723 exploitation signature — a FastJson '@type' key co-occurring with a jar:/ldap:/rmi: remote-resource URL or the JdbcRowSetImpl/dataSourceName lookup class — confirmed by Imperva's advisory and the public jsontype RCE lab. Only expressible on WAF/proxy telemetry that captures request bodies; endpoint EDR/FDR do not ship HTTP bodies, hence Defender/Falcon/Datadog/CloudWatch left empty. Cross-checked against: • https://www.imperva.com/blog/imperva-customers-protected-against-cve-2026-16723-critical-fastjson-1-x-zero-day-rce/ • https://github.com/alibaba/fastjson2/wiki/Security-Advisory:-Remote-Code-Execution-in-fastjson-1.2.68%E2%80%931.2.83 • https://github.com/dinosn/fastjson-jsontype-rce-lab
ATT&CKT1190
Data sourcesWeb.Web
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Security scanners / DAST tools (Burp, Nessus, Nuclei) probing for fastjson with @type test payloads
  • Legitimate APIs that accept a client-supplied field literally named 'type' where the value contains a jar: or ldap: URI
  • Internal red-team / BAS (Picus, SafeBreach) exercises replaying deserialization payloads
  • Log-shipping of stored @type strings in JSON documents that are echoed back into request URLs
Suppression filter
| where not (RequestURL has_any ("nuclei","nessus") or Message has_any ("nuclei","nessus") or SourceIP in ("10.0.0.0/8"))
Response runbook
1) Triage: pull the full request from the WAF/proxy for the matched SourceIP; confirm the body contains @type plus a remote jar:/ldap:/rmi: URL and identify the DestinationHostName Spring Boot app and its FastJson version (1.2.68-1.2.83?). 2) Contain: block the SourceIP at the WAF, enable FastJson SafeMode (-Dfastjson.parser.safeMode=true) on the target app, and isolate the app host if outbound class-load already occurred. 3) Hunt: pivot to UC 'Java outbound LDAP/RMI' and 'Java fat-JAR spawning shell' on the destination host within a 5-minute window of the request to confirm code execution.

Spring Boot Java fat-JAR spawning shell/recon child process (FastJson CVE-2026-16723 RCE) AIExploitation High
Detects a Java process launched as a Spring Boot executable fat-jar (java -jar xxx.jar) spawning cmd/powershell/sh/bash or a recon binary — the post-exploitation payload of CVE-2026-16723 landing on the app server. Article-specific: it requires the '-jar' parent context Alibaba names as the sole deployment prerequisite. Rationale: Anchors on Alibaba's stated prerequisite — a Spring Boot executable fat-jar (java -jar xxx.jar) — as the parent, paired with a shell/recon child, which is the concrete RCE outcome of CVE-2026-16723. Parent+child pairing keeps FP low versus a bare java or bare powershell query. Cross-checked against: • https://thehackernews.com/2026/07/fastjson-1x-rce-vulnerability-targeted.html • https://github.com/alibaba/fastjson2/wiki/Security-Advisory:-Remote-Code-Execution-in-fastjson-1.2.68%E2%80%931.2.83 • https://github.com/dinosn/fastjson-jsontype-rce-lab
ATT&CKT1190 T1203 T1059
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Jenkins/GitLab/TeamCity build agents (Java) legitimately invoking sh/bash/cmd for build steps
  • Java-based application servers shelling out to certutil/curl for cert or health-check tasks
  • Elastic/Logstash Java agents spawning helper processes
  • Admins running gradlew/mvnw wrappers that fork shells from a java parent
  • Monitoring tooling (Java) calling nslookup/ping for connectivity checks
Suppression filter
| where not (InitiatingProcessCommandLine has_any ("jenkins","gitlab-runner","teamcity","elastic-agent","logstash") or ProcessCommandLine has_any ("gradlew","mvnw"))
Response runbook
1) Triage: capture InitiatingProcessCommandLine to confirm the fat-jar name and whether the child cmdline shows recon/download (whoami, curl to external IP); correlate with any inbound @type WAF hit on the same host within minutes. 2) Contain: isolate the app server, kill the java parent, and apply FastJson SafeMode or migrate to fastjson2 (no vendor patch exists). 3) Hunt: on the same host review DeviceNetworkEvents for outbound LDAP/RMI (UC below) and any dropped .class/.jar in temp, and sweep the fleet for the same fat-jar name running vulnerable FastJson 1.2.68-1.2.83.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("java.exe","javaw.exe","java")
| where InitiatingProcessCommandLine has "-jar"
| where FileName in~ ("cmd.exe","powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","sh","bash","dash","whoami.exe","whoami","net.exe","curl.exe","curl","wget","certutil.exe","bitsadmin.exe","nslookup.exe","ping.exe","id","uname")
| where InitiatingProcessAccountName !endswith "$"
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, InitiatingProcessAccountName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, FileName, ProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessFolderPath, SHA256
| order by Timestamp desc
ImProcessCreate
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where ParentProcessName has_any ("java.exe","javaw.exe","/java")
| where ParentProcessCommandLine has "-jar"
| where ActingProcessName has_any ("cmd.exe","powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","/sh","/bash","/dash","whoami","net.exe","curl","wget","certutil.exe","bitsadmin.exe","nslookup.exe")
| project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, ActorUsername, ParentProcessCommandLine, ActingProcessName, ActingProcessCommandLine
| order by TimeGenerated desc
